speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Would the minister confirm or deny a report that 14 Cubans left a Czechoslovakian airliner recently at the international airport at Gander, Newfoundland, making a total of more than 100 who have defected from aircraft there, and after being held by immigration authorities for 24 hours were transferred to immigration department detention quarters at Halifax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: GANDER, NFLD.    DEFECTION OF CUBANS FROM CZECH PLANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for giving notice of this question. The report is substantially correct. Fourteen Cubans left a Czechoslovak airliner at Gander airport on September 5. This brings to over 100 the number of persons who have left aircraft at Gander in this way in the past two years.
No decisions have as yet been made in these 14 cases. In accordance with normal procedure, an immigration hearing is convened in each case in order to obtain full particulars of the individual and his intentions. Some of these people wish to go to other countries, while others seek to remain in Canada. Those wishing to go elsewhere are put in touch with the authorities of the countries concerned. The cases of those seek-


ing to stay in Canada are referred to Ottawa where I have the ultimate responsibility to decide whether to grant landed immigrant status or to allow the individual to stay under the authority of a minister's permit.
Pending final decisions the individuals concerned are accommodated in immigration quarters at Halifax or elsewhere.

whether the minister will be making a statement on this item.

I had hoped, Mr. Chairman, some time before the day was over to make a statement which would incorporate whatever replies I could make to the observations of hon. members. In that way I would be sure to talk about the things members were interested in, and not just things that I was interested in.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks at the very outset of the consideration of the Department of Transport's estimates. I am very pleased that we should be examining these estimates, since the present minister has been in function for quite some time.
Having had the privilege of being minister of transport, I must say that I consider it the most interesting department in the whole federal administration. There has often been talk of dividing it, but I am convinced that the present minister would be very disappointed if such a decision was made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I bring to the attention of hon. members that it is very noisy and difficult for the Chair to follow the remarks of the hon. member who has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I am of the opinion that it is possible at the present time to run the Department of Transport without dividing it. But, and this is a personal opinion, I believe that it would make sense to take the management of the civil aviation division away from the Department of Transport. However, we must wait for the decision of the government before making any comment in that regard.
Mr. Chairman, the day after his swearing in, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) made a great play about a plan to give Canada, at long last, a national policy with regard to civil aviation. Everyone was very interested to learn that the minister was undertaking such a large scale project. Though couched in a rather mysterious language, the plan had roused everyone's attention.
Yet, for the information of those who followed the work accomplished within the Department of Transport in matters of civil aviation, I must say that since then, we had cause for wondering what the minister meant by "national civil aviation policy". We also have every reason to wonder why the minister reversed his decision. Could it be that he has abandoned that project he had announced with such fanfare? Indeed, as far as our two large international air lines are concerned, that is, Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines, the only achievement in that direction we were able to see to date was the meetings of the two presidents at the minister's suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that the minister told the presidents of those two companies: "Now be good boys and try and get along together. Make an effort to see each other more often. There is really no problem; try to agree. Take your time, and we shall see how things stand later".
That is about all the national civil aviation policy that applies to those two large international lines.
At the time when the minister announced this new national civil aviation policy, the papers speculated quite a bit and wondered whether the minister meant that those two great lines would amalgamate, or whether Canada would decide to have one single large international service for all our international airways. The matter still comes up from time to time in the papers. We see some efforts being made in one direction or other, and I think that the house would be interested to know the present situation, because it is about time to put a stop to those rumours. Clearing up the matter in that way would give a certain peace of mind to the employees of those two companies, while allowing the directors of the two great international lines to progress and make plans for the years to come.
There is no doubt that during the last months, the two big international air lines have had very good financial results and that they are still bringing the name of Canada to the fore in the field of international air transport.
About the same time, the minister also announced great and mysterious plans concerning local air lines. There again, we have seen, as yet, no concrete results. As a matter of fact, newspapers reported that the minister had given to understand that the big air lines would probably have to give up some of their air routes for the benefit of local carriers.
For my part, I have not yet seen a single result of that project. If there have been any, I feel the minister should tell the house about them. There is no doubt that, when he made his statement, everyone interested in civil aviation in Canada saw in it the announcement of a new policy and then eagerly awaited the results.
Now, I recall that when I was minister of transport the opposition of the day was most critical of Canada's position, as compared to that of the United States, with regard to the bilateral agreements on civil aviation between our two countries.
Supply-Transport
I must confess that, in my capacity as minister, I was in no way satisfied with the situation. Our big air lines were undoubtedly quite right in insisting that the government make representations to the United States government, in order to improve the unfavourable position in which our two air lines found themselves compared to the American air lines.
Those bilateral agreements had been made by the previous government. We had to put up with those agreements and when we were in office, we made representations time and again to the American authorities on this matter.
I remember that during the last election campaign, the Liberal party said that if they were in office, they would settle the matter quickly and to the benefit of our air lines. Of course, there were meetings between our Canadian experts and the American experts, following a report to the President of the United States by Mr. Galbraith, the economist of international reputation. But up to the present, those discussions between our two countries have been unfruitful and we do not see what happy effects they might have for Canada.
I hope that during this debate the Minister of Transport will be able to report on this matter and announce certain progress, because it is very painful to see the position of both our great air lines as compared with the American companies.
When he answers those various questions, I would like the minister to give us his viewpoint with respect to the statement of the president of Air Canada the last time he appeared before the committee of the house, which goes into the financial report of that company.
The president of Air Canada actually stated that one of the reasons why he has always been in favour of a single international air line for Canada is the fact that to have two big lines in Canada placed our country in an inferiority position each time bilateral agreements have to be discussed with other nations. He gave as an example the discussions which were under way at that time between the United States and Canada.
To my mind that was an extremely important statement, and I believe the minister should tell us if the fact that we have two air lines in Canada is endangering our position.
According to my information, which is unofficial of course, the representatives of both air lines, who are in Washington as observers.

Supply-Transport
seem to get along fine at those talks. Therefore, I think the president of Air Canada has exaggerated the facts.
I think there ought to be an agreement between the two air lines, just as there are agreements between our two national railways.
It is absolutely ridiculous to think that we are not taking advantage of our rights.
For instance, Canada has the right to carry passengers, by virtue of what is called the five freedoms, between Paris and Rome. That is a route of very heavy traffic and all large carriers in the world make tremendous profits from it. But because of the relationship between our two main air lines, neither one is using that route which we are entitled to use.
You only have to imagine, for instance, the number of people who travel between Paris and Rome on the occasion of imposing ceremonies and large meetings like the ecumenical council in Rome. On that occasion, a great number of Canadian clergy go to Rome via Paris where they have to transfer to European carriers. It is so much income lost to Canadian air lines.
There is something else which could be to the advantage of our country. For instance, at this time, one of our two air lines has a flight to Tokyo and Hong Kong. If there could be an agreement between our two large carriers concerning the route between New York and Toronto, we could advertise, in New York, that the shortest route between New York and Tokyo is the one used by Canadian air lines that can fly north through Toronto, Vancouver, Alaska and land in Japan. But we are deprived of this advantage precisely because of the failure to agree between our two large air lines.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to labour the point too long, but I must say that I am very anxious to hear what the minister will have to say.
While we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Transport, I should like to raise a point which has already been mentioned many times in the house in the form of questions on the orders of the day.
I am thinking of the passenger service between airports and cities. In my opinion, the problem is most serious and I am not blaming the present government more than any other, but I feel that the public is now at a great disadvantage. We have reached a point where the companies which transport passengers between the airports and the cities charge so much that their fares are very often more expensive than plane fares.

I think the department should fully investigate this situation.
Since exclusive rights are involved in this matter, I feel they should not take advantage of this monopoly to increase their rates, but on the contrary, their rates should be lower than those of companies providing regular city transportation services, and I mean taxis.
At the present time, air passengers may take either a limousine or a taxi. People who ride in those limousines lose a great deal of time, because they are extremely slow and never start on time. Fares charged are rather expensive and there are only a few scheduled stops. From there, one has to take a taxi, and all this costs a lot of money. One has the choice to do that or to take taxis which are also exclusive, because they belong to the same company as the limousines and those taxis charge really prohibitive fares.
I think an investigation should be made in this field. An agreement should be concluded between provinces and municipalities, in order to abolish that monopoly and allow anyone who has a taxi permit in a province or municipality to go to the airport and freely serve the public. On the other hand, I know that it is easy to argue that there is a contract and nothing can be done, but I feel that those companies have gone too far. A few years ago it may have been necessary for those companies to have a franchise but this reason is no longer valid at the present time.
In my opinion, that system works against the passengers. I feel that the Department of Transport must intervene to protect the public whenever agreements carrying exclusive rights are prejudicial to passengers.
Mr. Chairman, I should not want to take too much of the committee's time but, before I sit down, I should like to say a few words about shipbuilding in Canada and for Canada.
I remember that, in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) expressed very serious doubts about the value and especially the advantages of grants to the Canadian shipbuilding industry.
I see that this government has maintained our policy. I am sure that after holding his portfolio for a few months, the Minister of Transport has decided to continue those grants which are absolutely necessary, in my opinion.
The subsidies were very useful. We owe them our merchant marine on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes, which will be entirely modernized and up to date.
Thanks to those subsidies and to this merchant marine we were able to find enough

space to ship from the lakehead to the St. Lawrence ports tremendous loads of wheat and grain to Russia and other countries behind the iron curtain, as well as to China.
Had we not followed such a policy at that time, grain shipping would certainly have been delayed, with disastrous results for our western farmers and for this country as a whole.
We had also taken action to keep or reserve the use of Canada's inland waters only for ships flying the Canadian flag. We had obtained the agreement of all other commonwealth countries signatories to the commonwealth agreement on coastal traffic, and we were about to introduce legislation to this effect when, unfortunately, an election was called and our program was interrupted. I hope that the present government will not hesitate to maintain that policy, in order to give new strength to our merchant marine. It is unfortunate for our country that our merchant marine never had that new vitality which would enable us to have a real seagoing merchant marine.
In my opinion, the government should endeavour to take further steps in order to reach this goal completely.
I believe that, in another field of concern to Canadian shipping the government should do more. And here I am talking about the trips organized each summer to ship food and equipment to our various stations in the far north.
These trips should be restricted to ships under the Canadian flag. At present, the government charters foreign ships. To my mind, this is a discrimination against our ship owners and our seamen. I really believe that this is a field where the government has full authority and for which it pays all expenditures and signs contracts with the shipowners. Consequently, it should limit its naval operations to ships under Canadian flag. It is a new step toward the building of a Canadian merchant marine of significance.
Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat, I would like once again to draw the attention of the house on the serious problem of Canadian waters.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) directed a question to the Minister of Transport; the latter expressed his concern at the seriouness of this problem. I am convinced, as every other sincere Canadian, that the minister is really worried over this great problem threatening our main natural resource.
Supply-Transport
Today, those who have an opportunity to see the St. Lawrence river find out to what extent the waters are low and polluted all along its banks. Anyone seeing the St. Lawrence at the present time may realize the importance and the urgency of this problem, as well as the pressing need for a new system under which this problem would be no longer in the hands of bureaucracy, and when I say "bureaucracy" I do not mean the civil service. But this article, which was written by Mr. Arthur Blakeley, of the Gazette, depicts perfectly the situation prevailing in that field, and, in my opinion, it is a hair-raising problem for those really concerned.
There are at least some 30 officials in the federal government who meddle with this problem. There is no agreement between them, the reports of their discussions are lost or get shelved in some branch or other; different policies are adopted. I believe that the government should take the bull by the horns, that
is,	establish a department of water courses in Canada, or set up an agency, some administrative body which would have the necessary authority to study the problems as a whole and to make really serious decisions.
An engineer was telling me recently that in Canada we waste to such an extent these natural resources that if we keep on doing
it,	the ocean-going vessels will probably be unable to go upstream further than Quebec.
I think that one of the most serious gaps in our past is not to have developed hydraulic engineering. All the people who had to carry out projects along the St. Lawrence river were civil engineers who, though very well qualified in their field, were by no means specialized in hydraulics.
Thus, all along the St. Lawrence river, seaports and jetties were built and dikes were erected without worrying too much about the effect of those constructions on the tides, the currents and ice movements. This resulted in a complete change in the currents of the St. Lawrence, and today, the water is so low that ships cannot come up to Montreal to take on a full cargo. And there is another aspect. The water of the St. Lawrence is so polluted all along its course, that people living in those magnificent summer residences and resorts cannot swim or bathe there. Today all that is finished, everything has been wasted. No doctor will advise anybody to bathe in the St. Lawrence river.
I believe that the federal government, even if it is not the only one to blame, should convene a federal-provincial conference on this matter and tackle the problem, because

Supply-Transport
today, the Ottawa and the St. Lawrence are practically open sewers. This situation has lasted long enough, and it is imperative for the government to assume its responsibilities, forget what happened in the past, and take an entirely new attitude. There is no question of blaming this or that person or body, but the problem must be tackled if we want the St. Lawrence river to remain that magnificent waterway which was the cradle of this country.
I refer to the St. Lawrence because I know it well, having been raised in Three Rivers.
I know that the great lakes are experiencing the same difficulty. As for lake Huron, the situation is critical and the government must do something about it. That is why I was so pleased by the minister's answer to my hon. friend from Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler). I hope the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) will take positive action, leaving political manoeuvring aside. Any positive step he takes to help the Canadian people in this connection will be wholeheartedly supported by the opposition.
That will conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, and I thank hon. members for their attention. I hope that, when all the other hon. members have made their speeches, the minister will answer the few questions I have put to him.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is displaying what he considers an admirable reticence in opening the estimates of his department. He has indicated he would prefer to listen to what some other members might have to say. However I think I should say at the outset that some of us are anxious to hear something from the minister before these estimates are concluded. He has been a member of this house long enough to know that members have an understandable interest in the attitudes of a new minister with respect to various matters of policy. Certainly there are a number of matters upon which I should like to have the benefit of the thinking of the Minister of Transport as we begin the spending for a new fiscal year of this very important Department of Transport. I have some questions I should like to pose or at least some matters I should like to draw to the minister's attention at this stage upon which I should like to have a statement from him prior to the conclusion of these estimates. Actually, I would prefer that he might deal with them when we are giving consideration to the various sections of the estimates, at which time there may be a

better opportunity for questioning him on these points.
If I may I should like to take a few minutes to draw his attention to the particular areas of interest I have immediately before me, so far as the estimates of his department are concerned this year. I might tell the minister that there were a number of matters about which I had some discussion with his immediate predecessor in the portfolio. One of them had to do with the operations of the air transport board. The former minister and I had a number of discussions on this subject last year. Amongst other things, I was then urging that the air transport board should adopt a procedure of going much closer to the people than it had done in the past in respect of the holding of public hearings concerning the establishment of lines or rates. I should like to tell the minister I was very happy that, in connection with its regional hearings, the air transport board did see fit to hold sittings in some of the smaller centres along the coast of British Columbia. While I have had it reported to me that the citizens did not flock to those hearings in large numbers to make representations, nevertheless I think that whatever decision the air transport board may have arrived at in connection "with various matters in relation to the changing of existing air line routes, there will likely be a more ready acceptance of the board's decision than there was in relation to certain matters not too long ago. There was certainly a strong protest, as the minister is aware, concerning certain actions taken by the board in connection with air lines.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that, arising out of a certain situation that developed in respect of a decision of the board last year, I came to feel there was a rather serious flaw in the existing Aeronautics Act which, as the minister will recall, provides that if an air line which has an application before the board is not satisfied with the board's decision, an appeal to the minister does lie. However in the case of another air line, if it feels its interests have been advertently affected by a decision of the board no such appeal to the minister does lie under the terms of the law at the moment. On the face of it, this seems to be a rather unfair situation. I am hoping that when the minister is able to proceed with the amendments to the Aeronautics Act, which are now on the order paper in the form of a resolution, this particular point will not be overlooked in those amendments.

I did have some discussions on this very point with his predecessor, and it was suggested to me that when the Aeronautics Act was up for amendment it might be appropriate for me to pursue my argument in this connection. I should like to suggest to the minister that if this particular point is not already covered in the amendments which he intends to introduce, this is something to which he should give serious consideration. I suppose there is a question which can arise as to whether or not there should be any appeal to the minister. If there is to be an appeal allowed to the minister under the legislation, certainly so far as I am concerned it should not be a one way street. In other words, both parties should have the right to appeal.
While I am on the question of air transport, Mr. Chairman, I should like to indicate also to the minister that I am very much concerned about the type of facilities which can and should be developed for the landing of planes on water. I think it is generally recognized in this house that a great many millions of dollars have been spent on facilities for passengers to be transferred by air in connection with planes which land on the land. Most members of the house have had some opportunity to take advantage of the facilities which are provided at some of our more modern air terminals where we have, in general terms, very complicated and expensive technical facilities provided to assure that passengers will arrive at these terminals in safety and comfort. The whole question of seaplane landing facilities is a neglected one, so far as the Department of Transport and parliament are concerned. I only hope that because of the nature of his constituency the minister may be inclined to have a greater appreciation of this matter than some of his predecessors.
I had an opportunity of pointing out a few things to the minister's immediate predecessor during a visit he made to the B.C. coast. I was able to explain to him some of the landing problems that arise due to winds and tides, because I had personal experience of the hazards that develop when landing a seaplane in places where there are protruding piles against which winds may swing aircraft wings. As compared with the provision of facilities for landing planes in other parts of the country, very little has been done to develop such facilities along our sea coasts. I have had some discussions on this matter with persons operating planes along the B.C. coast, so the minister will not
Supply-Transport
be surprised when I tell him the B.C. aviation council sent me a copy of a recent communication they forwarded to him. I would like him to tell us his reactions to the suggestions made by that council.
I believe that under former policies the department spent more money on the establishment of landing facilities than circumstances justified. All those interested in this problem on the Pacific coast are anxious that the best possible facilities be provided at the lowest possible cost. We are convinced that with proper correlation between the marine services branch of the department and the planning sections of the Department of Public Works adequate seaplane landing facilities can be provided in many areas where none presently exist, at a very modest cost-modest compared with the amount spent on the provision of landing facilities for land based aircraft.
I am particularly interested in the levying of wharfage charges and I hope the minister will deal with this matter when we reach the marine services branch estimates. As the minister may recall, I had a recent exchange of correspondence with him on this subject, and he sent me an explanatory statement outlining the basis on which these charges are currently being levied, under the regulations which came into effect last January 23.
In this statement the minister enunciated the idea that those who use these facilities should be prepared to pay something for the service provided. Not many responsible people would quarrel with that idea, but having examined his explanatory statement I do not feel we have arrived at a proper and satisfactory arrangement. As a matter of fact I think the regulations seek to impose an impossible responsibility on the administrative officers in the field, and that the policy is impossible of being equitably applied.
I have received complaints concerning these charges for use of the harbour installations at Comox, and I would point out there are a great many places which have these facilities but where there are no wharfingers to collect the wharfage charges. If I understand the regulations correctly there is a certain onus on people using these facilities to regard the district marine agent as a wharfinger, where there is no wharfinger as such, but I do not know how the minister can expect a fisherman who has tied up in port at Whaletown or Namu to send in a report later, saying he was tied up there for

Supply-Transport
10 hours and including the money for the wharfage charges.
I cite Comox as an illustration. There are several installations within a relatively few miles of Comox where no charges are being levied. An attempt is being made to apply the charges in Comox, where there is a wharfinger. I do not intend to be critical of the wharfinger, but with the situation under which he operates he cannot be regarded as a full time employee. I am informed that certain boats which the wharfinger knows will be moored there are charged wharfage, but other boats come in, in some cases yachts operated by people who can well afford to pay wharfage charges, and these boats may stay there a day or two, and then away they go and no charges are levied against them. As the minister will readily understand, this is creating an attitude of resentment against the whole idea.
In addition I should advise the minister that the local business people in Comox rely almost entirely upon the business which commercial fishermen and other boat owners bring to them, and these business people are resentful because they feel this arrangement is driving people away from Comox harbour, and that boats are going elsewhere where no charges are levied. So, while I have some sympathy with the minister in his attempt to formulate an integrated policy with respect to a difficult question, I wish nevertheless to register my own feeling that a better solution could be reached than the one now adopted. It is my view that ports in the category of Comox, which I have used as an example, should be excluded from the application of the regulations.
I had hoped for an opportunity during the summer recess of spending a good deal of time discussing this question with commercial fishermen and other boat operators in the area for which I have the greatest concern.
I am sure the hon. member will permit me to say that I, too, shared that hope.

Perhaps it would not be amiss to take this opportunity to point out that one of the most important functions of a member of parliament in my view, and apparently in the view of the minister as well, is to ascertain the views of his constituents, particularly in areas where the operations of some of the government departments are of such great importance in the daily lives of the people. One of our most important responsi-

bilities, I feel, is to talk to the people we represent and ascertain their views as to how some of these matters should be dealt with. It is a matter of great regret to me that I have not had such an opportunity during the current year and the minister would no doubt agree with me that a Christmas recess, if we get one, does not fall at the time of year when it is easiest to do a job of this kind.
Nevertheless I have had some opportunity to discuss this question with the people who are most directly involved and the general reaction, at least among the more responsible minded of those to whom I spoke, seemed to be this: They had no objection to the idea of paying some reasonable charge where adequate facilities were provided, particularly in places where light, power, water and supervision were at the disposal of people needing these services. However in cases where these services have not been available and where no charges have been made in the past, there is a natural reluctance to accept any additional cost.
One or two suggestions have been made to me as alternatives to the idea presently advanced as the basis for wharfage charges. I will put them before the committee, not because I am persuaded they are correct or that they are necessarily better than the present arrangements, but because they have been made to me and because they are worthy of consideration. One such proposal is that instead of attempting to levy a charge in accordance with the length of the vessel to be moored, a small tax might be placed on fuel, say one cent a gallon. Another suggestion made to me is that it might be possible to issue an annual mooring licence. Commercial fishermen, when they went to obtain their commercial licences, could, if they intended to use public mooring facilities, pay a mooring charge in accordance with the size of their vessels. In return they would receive licences to moor at any of the public facilities they wished to use as they voyaged up and down the coast. I have not yet reached any final conclusion as to the merits of these two suggestions, but the minister should be thinking along these lines as he tries to work out a more satisfactory policy than the present arrangement is proving to be on the coast of British Columbia. I will leave it to the hon. gentleman to make his own analysis of how these charges should apply on the coast of Newfoundland.
There are a great number of questions one can always discuss in connection with the operations of a department whose work

spreads over a spectrum as broad as that of the Department of Transport. I should like the minister, before this discussion ends, to give us the latest information about what is developing in the field of policy with regard to cable television. This is a subject which has come up on a number of occasions during the life of this parliament and it is, of course, a matter of concern to a large number of people. I have made my own position clear. As far as I am concerned I do not believe there should be any attempt to restrict artificially the right of people to view the programs of their own choice. I think any attempt to do so is neither necessary nor desirable. Indeed, it could easily become a form of censorship. If we want to encourage Canadians to watch Canadian programs, the best way of doing it is to make Canadian programs so attractive that viewers will not want to watch programs from the United States or any other country, exclusively at least.
I believe there is nothing wrong in seeing what United States television can produce. Indeed I hope the day will come when we shall have much more ready access to television programs from Britain and other European countries than we have at the present time. It is also my belief that the need does exist for programs on the air which have a basically Canadian flavour and content if we are to survive as a nation. With regard to cable television, however, I would point out that in some areas of my constituency at least, due to the geography of the coast line, the only programs available are those which originate in the United States, and even these can only be received through the use of special antennae with cable connections to individual sets. I hope the minister will make it clear that there is no intention on the part of the government to restrict artificially the right of people in situations such as these to view such programs as they are able to receive in present circumstances.
While I am on this subject, Mr. Chairman, I should like to urge upon the minister, as a member of the government, the necessity of taking steps so that parliament may provide a much more adequate budget for the provision of Canadian radio and television, so that those who represent constituencies like mine will no longer receive from the C.B.C. the answer we have had again and again, "If you people will provide us with the money, we will extend facilities to these areas", namely those areas in which Canadians cannot now satisfactorily receive C.B.C. programs. Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I will withdraw from the discussion, temporarily at
Supply-Transport
least, and hope to have some comments from the minister as we get further along into the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, during consideration of the Department of Transport's estimates, I think the occasion is well chosen to draw to the attention of the hon. members a few problems in which I have been personally interested for some time and which concern not only the people of the riding of Quebec-Montmorency but also the people of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole.
I avail myself of the fact that item 1 allows us to discuss those problems in the house. Most of those problems have been submitted by myself to various organizations coming under the Department of Transport, and the answers have always been unsatisfactory, inadequate or non-existent.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I feel it is my duty and in the interest of the citizens concerned to draw these problems to the attention of the hon. members.
I would like to speak of the Canadian National Railways Company and of Air Canada. Those two crown corporations must report yearly to the railways, canals and telegraph lines standing committee or to the sessional committee. Since I have been in parliament, I have noticed that the evidence given by the representatives of those various companies, either the president of the Canadian National Railways Company or the president of Air Canada, were not at all satisfactory. They often declined to answer questions, or else they took refuge behind a kind of immunity by saying that it was not customary to disclose certain figures, etc., so that, even under our democratic system, we are unable to scrutinize the budget and the expenditures of those two crown corporations.
I realize that, as it has already been pointed out, it would be practically impossible for those companies to operate if members of this house were to question them repeatedly, if not every day, to find out just how they are running their business. And it is also said that, inasmuch as those crown corporations have to compete with other companies, certain figures ought not to be revealed, since that would be detrimental to those crown corporations. Considering that those two companies are subsidized by the government, that taxpayers help to make up for their deficits, it would not make sense to enable private enterprises to benefit from confidential information. Of course, we have to agree with that line

Supply-Transport
of reasoning. Yet, just because of the terms imposed by the crown corporations, the Canadian taxpayer is absolutely helpless, as he has never at any time been able to obtain satisfactory answers. The taxpayer may not be exactly familiar with the procedures and ways of those two crown corporations, nor with any possible schemes with other people set up with the help of officers in those corporations.
I remember, some time ago, having asked a question when the C.N.R. president was before the committee. I asked him then-though I knew very well that he would not be able to give an immediate answer-what was the distribution of traffic, at the Palais station in Quebec city, as between the C.N.R. and the C.P.R.; furthermore in what proportion premises were occupied by the C.N.R. and by the C.P.R., and finally what costs were charged to the C.N.R. for the use of those services. Mr. Gordon told me that he could not give me an answer, but would see to it that I get one later on. And I heard absolutely nothing until, following a second letter of mine, I received on Sept. 4, from the Canadian National Railways, a letter with figures indicating that, at least to uninitiated eyes, like mine, the C.N.R., to a certain extent, helps out the C.P.R. by making much less use of tracks and premises than the latter company, although expenses are apportioned roughly on a fifty-fifty basis between the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. This means that the C.N.R. is contributing, with the taxpayers' money, to bolster the C.P.R.'s profits.
These is nothing wrong, of course, in the C.N.R. doing the C.P.R. a good turn. But when we know that the taxpayers have to make up the deficits, I think the C.N.R.'s expenditures should be looked into more closely. That is the kind of information we cannot obtain from the presidents of those companies when they come before the committee.
If I had not insisted on a reply, I think I would still be in the dark as to the conditions of the contract signed in that connection by the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. However, some lines have been abandoned following the signing of the contract.
Certain trains have stopped using the C.P.R. tracks. Others follow a new route; instead of passing through Quebec city, they take another C.N.R. track which brings them directly to St. Raymond. Those are all services for which the C.N.R. has paid for and which are no longer used. In fact, I wonder if the C.N.R. still pays the C.P.R. the same charges and rent as before.
All that to say that unless we remain on our toes, the Canadian taxpayers will practically find themselves under the domination of certain private companies.
There would still be lots of things to say in that connection. For instance, last year, I asked questions about the Canadian Prepack and the Crowley McCraken companies, which deal either directly or indirectly with the C.N.R. and with which the crown corporation has contracts which cannot be scrutinized because they are private contracts. It is impossible to know either the names of the directors of those companies because the latter are incorporated under provincial law.
Those are all factors which make it difficult to examine the budget and expenses of the C.N.R. and, occasionally also, of Air Canada.
I still have other observations to make in this regard which are even more serious inasmuch as they refer to what is apparently a matter of political patronage.
Shame.
I know the minister will be quite surprised to learn that such a thing as political patronage could exist within his department-
Shame.

-because it would just about be the only place where it could be found, since we know none exists elsewhere. Here, I wish to refer to another company called Transol Inc. I had asked the C.N.R. what agreements they had reached with that company. I was told that the C.N.R. had not sold any property to Transol. Of course, that was not what I meant and I had to give it another try, for even if I knew the answer, I wanted to get it directly from the C.N.R. So I made another attempt and asked them more specifically what transportation contracts Transol Inc. had been awarded between Levis and Riviere du Loup.
I finally succeeded in getting an answer, on September 10, from the secretary of the company, Mr. Vaughn. Now, this is a contract signed by the C.N.R. with that company, whose directors are Mr. Marius Diamant, Mr. Gaston Desjardins, a lawyer, and I think one of his associates, Mr. Ovide Laflamme, whom I have not met but who ran against me in the last election.
This company offered its services to the C.N.R. The latter investigated the credit standing of the Transol Inc. company in order to know what it was worth. According to the

report submitted to the C.N.R., that company was not solvent, it was not in operation and was only incorporated on June 13, 1963, which meant that it was quite newly formed and had no capital value. Strange enough, in spite of this unfavourable report, the C.N.R. decided to award the contract to the Transol Inc. company, so that the latter is now operating a freight transportation service between its stations located between Levis and Riviere du Loup.
Transol Inc. was authorized to operate this service by the Quebec transport board on October 30, 1963, and only started operating on that date.
As can be easily imagined, this means that when the company was awarded a contract by the C.N.R. for freight transportation, bank credits were unfrozen, so to speak, and it was very easy for this company to secure from the bank the funds necessary to set up the whole system as we know it today.
This even enabled this company to purchase a tank-truck in order to transport wine from Niagara Falls, this wine producing area we know quite well, to Quebec city, for the Quebec liquor control board. This means that this transportation company competed directly with the Canadian National Railways, which already had tank cars, and that the crown corporation consequently lost this contract to Transol Inc.
Evidently, in regard to the province of Quebec, the same thing happens. The liquor board is a crown corporation, so to say, which is entirely above politics. It then became quite easy for that corporation to send in a tender to the liquor board. However, C.N.R., which had agreed, as it were, to the creation of such a corporation, lost the contract they had with the Quebec liquor board.
To my mind it is a loathesome situation when a company such as the C.N.R. whose deficits, as I said, are made up by the people of Canada, is at the mercy of a small group like that.
Coming back to the directors of Transol Inc., lawyers Gaston Desjardins and Ovide Laflamme have their office in the same building as Mr. Gerard Levesque who used to be chairman of the Quebec Liberal federation.
He used to be.

Yes, he used to be chairman of the federation. He did a lot of work at that time. There was another person in that office, Mr. Laurent P. Bolduc, who is not a lawyer, I think, but who owns two ships, the Sillery and the Cacouna, the building of
Supply-Transport
which was largely paid through federal grants.
Consequently, that is a fairly great concentration of power. I am sure the minister will get to the bottom of this so that there will be no repetition of such distasteful happenings.
Of course, now that Transol Inc. is a well organized company which is doing good business, I imagine it would be difficult to take away its contracts, but the minister will surely be on his guard the next time such a thing happens.
I would have other remarks to make in that connection but I will stop here. Naturally, I am not a minister but I have a rather thick file on that case.
Now I shall say a few words concerning another question, coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport, that is the choice of a medium range aircraft by Air Canada. This is another corporation entirely independent from the government and which receives no instructions from the latter; in brief, this is a company which makes its own decisions. Then, we have nothing to say. It is nevertheless strange to find out that the decision made previously to choose the BAC-111 aircraft was changed following the unfortunate accident suffered by the prototype plane while it was flying over a British city.
I feel that Air Canada was wise to change its decision, since it realized that the plane could be dangerous.
As far as the DC-9 is concerned, that plane was never built. It never flew once and it was accepted. And the Caravelle, which has proved itself over many years, is used quite extensively in the United States by a firm which is not particularly francophile and in a country which has no particular concessions to make to France. As a matter of fact, they are very happy to use the Caravelle because it gives very good service and its safety rating is very high.
Mr. Chairman, I will not talk about this any longer, because I do not want to reopen an old sore. I just wanted to point out some odd things that might be found in the management of Air Canada.
Another field which comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and which awakened my interest is that of radio and television. As a matter of fact, I always wondered why television and radio come under the Department of Transport, especially broadcasting stations and the issuance of licences and permits.

Supply-Transport
I know very well that permits for the operation of radio and television stations are issued by the Department of Transport, on the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors, although sometimes when the minister did not like the board of broadcast governors' decision, he changed it and went ahead with another policy that had not been recommended by the governors.
For a few years now I have been interested in a Gaspe peninsula television company, namely the "Compagnie de t.v.-transgaspe-sienne", which submitted to the board of broadcast governors rather long and detailed briefs that I have at hand. They are about four inches thick.
Following a decision that I never understood from the board of broadcast governors, that company was prevented from operating a television station in the north Gaspe area. The reasons given for this refusal were numerous and inconsistent. That company had the luck-or the bad luck-to submit briefs to the board of broadcast governors on four or five occasions.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member is aware that there are already two other television stations in the Gaspe peninsula, one in Matane and the other in Carleton, which serve the peninsula and must also, under their operating licence, serve that area. Besides, I feel that those companies give a very good service to the areas they cover.

Mr. Chairman, I was precisely coming to this point, because it is a complicated problem, in a complicated area, and a problem in which I have taken a complicated interest also.
If one studies the questions I put to the Department of Transport, both under this government and the previous one, one will realize that I did not envisage the question in a superficial way.
I know that the Matane station has moved its antenna. Instead of erecting it near the city of Matane, they went away and erected it on Logan mountain, in order to have a much wider field of action. However, this antenna was barely erected than a satellite had to be built on Climont mountain, because it was found that the city of Matane and the Matapedia valley could no longer be served adequately.

I feel that this is a very complicated question, and I think the decisions were made in favour of the existing stations.
I know that this is normal, that those stations have the right to have a monopoly, but on the other hand I know also that some areas in the Gaspe peninsula are entitled to service, and if those two stations had an exclusive contract with the C.B.C., the third station might have signed a contract with another company, with Tele-metropole, for instance.
And if people had not wanted Tele-metropole, the Trans-Gaspe t.v. company could have signed a new contract with the C.B.C. Anyway, the problem was not beyond solution.
If existing stations did not wish to make use of Jacques Cartier mountain, as did Trans-Gaspe t.v., it was hardly up to the latter to let the two existing companies benefit from the advantages offered by the highest peak in eastern Canada.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit another question?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, is the hon. member aware of the fact that, even if an antenna had been installed on Jacques Cartier mountain, the station established there would nevertheless have had to set up satellites to serve some villages along the north shore of the Gaspe peninsula?

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased that the hon. member asked this question.
The consulting engineer of Trans-Gaspe t.v., Mr. Boisvert, made a technological study of the power of the CKBL-TV Matane station, and stated, on the sole basis of mathematical computation, that the district around Matane would have a signal several decibels weaker and that the station would have to use a satellite further away, if the people on behalf of whom an operation permit had been sought were to have a proper service.
The predictions of this engineer have been found perfectly true.
The same engineer also studied the diffusion of waves from Jacques Cartier mountain to certain remote spots of the northern part of the Gaspe peninsula such as Gros Mome and Grande Vallee, for example, which are the most inaccessible. The report prepared by that qualified engineer indicated that the new station could serve those areas. The quality of the service would be somewhat inferior,

perhaps in the B or C grade, instead of A. But this would have been sufficient to enable the inhabitants of those areas to employ television adequately.
If an engineer who was sufficiently competent to predict the coverage of the CKBL-TV antenna feels that the station which could have been operated by Trans-Gaspe t.v. would have given satisfactory results, I do not see why those results should be discussed.
On the economic level, it is clear that the two stations now in operation would be greatly handicapped, especially on the north shore, since the greater percentage of the volume of business of the Matane t.v. company comes from the north shore.
Of course, I agree that the new station which could have been operated would have been prejudicial to the existing stations. The Magdalen islands and Anticosti island would probably have been served by the new station. Moreover, the north shore of the province of Quebec, the Natashquan area and the other areas located a little farther to the east, in short all the areas which are not now served by the Matane station, would have been served by the new one. This means that, as far as the technical aspect is concerned, the station which could have been operated by Trans-Gaspe t.v. is necessary.
It is obvious that certain companies may suffer some financial prejudice. I agree that the new station may constitute a handicap. But the strangest thing is that if we examine the objecting briefs, we realize that those companies presented divergent views to the board of broadcast governors. When the application for the establishment of a new station was presented, they told the board that they were in a bad financial situation and that they did not want a third station to compete with them. However, when the question was to expand or set up a new satellite station, they would say to the board that their finances were very good and that they could afford to make the necessary expenditures, consequently, the evidence was contradictory, and so were the decisions of the board of broadcast governors.
At first it was said that Trans-Gaspe t.v. did not fulfil the technical requirements. The latter then had to change the technical specifications so as to meet the requirements of the board of governors. When the officials of Trans-Gaspe t.v. came up with these new improvements, the decision of the board of governors was that their financial organization was not adequate. And when the officials came back again to show that their financial 20220-515
Supply-Transport
organization was adequate, the decision of the board of governors was that the existing stations had to be given an opportunity to install satellites and try to serve the Gaspe population.
I have nothing against the decisions of the board of governors; nor do I have anything to gain from the case of the Trans-Gaspe t.v. Company which I have put forward.
But I suggest that if that firm had been prevented, for whatever reason, to make those changes and reappear before the board of governors, about $50,000 or more would have been saved.
That company had always been given to understand that it would be permitted to set up a television station and, consequently, it spent a great deal of money. However, it is now in a hopeless situation, as no decision has been made.
Since the board of governors comes under the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) and the issuance of a licence is the responsibility of the Department of Transport, it makes matters more difficult.
I am not in the least exercising any pressure on the government to make a decision. I am only saying it should have been regarded as a matter of justice, for they let the Trans-Gaspe company go to a great deal of expense by leading it to believe it could set up a station. Now the company's request has been turned down. I think, Mr. Chairman, we have here a situation which is at least discriminatory. I know that some chambers of commerce exerted pressure against Trans-Gaspe t.v., while, at the same time, others protested in favour of the company and this made it even more difficult for the minister to reach a decision.
However, it is a question of justice. Trans-Gaspe t.v. acted in good faith in wanting to serve that part of Gaspe which has no service. This has always interested that company which has been operating, under another name, a community antenna and, for a long time, had decided to bring television to the people of Ste Anne des Monts and St. Joachim de Tourelle. I believe three or more stations were received by means of this antenna and programs were retransmitted locally to Ste Anne des Monts and vicinity. This proves that the company has always wished to serve adequately the people of that area.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister to take this matter into consideration. As I have said previously, I do not want to pressure him; nor do I want to force a decision on him. I

Supply-Transport
know that he is subject to very strong pressures from opposing camps. I know that financially, certain companies have made investments and, naturally, they do not like competition.
However, for the sake of justice and equity, the minister should make a decision, which would favour not only Trans-Gasp6 t.v. but the whole of the population of North Gaspe and even of other places, who could be served by this station which enjoys a very advantageous geographical location.
Before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word concerning a long lasting problem-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired. Does he have the unanimous consent of the house to continue his remarks?
Agreed.

I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I apologize to the house for taking up so much of its valuable time.
However, I am so concerned with these matters that I would not miss the opportunity to discuss them before the house, and I will try to be as brief as possible.
This, Mr. Chairman, is a matter which has not been discussed for a long time, that is the foreshore at Beaupre.
Theoretically, the foreshore belongs to the national harbours board which has jurisdiction over the port of Quebec. The board maintains that the foreshore is necessary to the expansion of the port of Quebec. Theoretically, it cannot give up the foreshore without prejudice to the good management of the port of Quebec.
Some private companies requested from Quebec harbour authorities permission to use part of the foreshore, to build a deep-water wharf enabling them to move a certain quantity of cement produced nearby.
Riparian proprietors have been using these lands for a certain number of years and, in many cases, they claim to own them. The national harbours board challenges these claims, saying that these lands belong to the crown and that nobody can use them without the consent of the national harbours board.
These lands are not put to any use, they are in a very poor state and they cannot be profitable to anybody, not even to the port of Quebec.
During a recent meeting of the mayors of the municipalities concerned, the possibility of developing the foreshore at Beaupre was discussed.

The suggestion was made that the national harbours board would purely and simply waive its claim, subject perhaps to some conditions, to the use of the foreshore. It would hand over to the municipalities concerned all the foreshore at Beaupre with permission to develop it as they pleased.
This means that certain municipalities could start some developments, such as parks or the like. Some municipalities could even use it to extend their territory and authorize the building of houses. Others could use them for commercial or industrial purposes.
I think the minister should give special consideration to this problem.
For a number of years, the people concerned have been seeing officials of the national harbours board about this, but no decision has ever been made in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Would he favour this idea, even if it is detrimental to the development of Quebec harbour?

Mr. Chairman, as I said a while ago, even though this land is essential, theoretically, to the development of Quebec harbour, in practice, on account of the limited budget of the national harbours board and of the very poor state of Quebec harbour, the sums of money that could be used for the development of the foreshore would be so large that we would probably have to wait another 50 years for Quebec harbour to expand along the Beaupr6 shore.
Mr. Chairman, I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport shaking his head, but that problem has been under consideration for the past 60 years at least.
We met several times with the Quebec harbour and the national harbours board officials in Ottawa, and no firm decision were ever made; the board officials never showed us any definite plan indicating their intention of developing that part of the coast at Beaupre. In that way and without causing any harm whatsoever to the Quebec harbour, the national harbours board could, especially if it were instructed to do so by the government, solve that problem to the advantage of everybody, including Quebec harbour, and particularly to the satisfaction of all concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank you and all hon. members for being kind enough to allow me to continue.
I hope that my comments will decide the minister to act in certain fields. Of course, I do not wish to insist, but as I said a short

time ago, I hope that he will take my remarks in due consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take a few minutes to comment on the estimates of the Department of Transport which, as we all know, is one of the most important.
I believe that the various organizations that come under this department are much too heavy for one man alone to carry. For example, among the branches that come under the Department of Transport, we find marine services, railways and steamships, civil aviation, telecommunications, meteorological services, air transport board, Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, Canadian maritime commission, national harbours board and the St. Lawrence seaway authority. The administration of those services is funnelled into the offices of the Department of Transport, and, frankly, it represents a task that is too heavy for one man. I would suggest, therefore, to the government that the department be divided into two parts.
Under the first part the following services could be included: marine services, railways and steamships, crown corporations such as the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, the Canadian maritime commission, the national harbours board and the St. Lawrence seaway authority.
The second part which could be called the department of air transport, would include the following: civil aviation, air transport board, telecommunications and meteorological services. This would make possible a more efficient performance by dividing the work within the department and by distributing the tasks more evenly.
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) mentioned a while ago, as regards passenger service between air terminals and cities-be it Montreal, Toronto or Quebec-I think those companies are exercising a monopoly and I agree with the hon. member when he said that an investigation should be made in this connection, and the Department of Transport should decide on a maximum and a minimum rate for the transportation of passengers between air terminals and the cities.
I have already made a recommendation to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines respecting handling of baggage in airports. I for one asked that at Ancienne Lorette airport, near Quebec city, where baggage is handled a little too roughly, carriages drawn by a tractor should be provided, instead of a type of tractor equipped with a box, to convey baggage from the planes to the airport.
Supply-Transport
I should also ask the minister whether it would be possible to use Vanguard aircraft on passenger services between Quebec and Ottawa. We have noticed on several occasions that travellers must make reservations several days in advance and often cannot get a seat on board because there are too many passengers. I ask the minister whether it would not be possible to replace the Viscount aircraft by Vanguards on the air route Quebec-Ottawa via Montreal.
Now, I should like to turn to another problem which I already raised in this house; I know that the parliamentary secretary is in a very good position to discuss that problem of railway crossings in Quebec city. We have in Quebec city a railway company, the Canadian Pacific, which operates a passenger service. The station is located in the business centre, and I think that besides being out of date, it interferes with the traffic and business in Quebec city. Passenger trains circulating between Quebec and Montreal must pass through the city from east to west or from west to east and thus cross the streets eight times in Quebec city. Now, six of those streets are located in the business sector, which means that every time a train goes in or out, a traffic jam is the result.
I wrote to Mr. Gordon, president of the C.N.R., in this connection in June 1963. Mr. Gordon answered that he was prepared to enter into discussions with the authorities of the Canadian Pacific, of the board of transport commissioners and of the Department of Transport, in order to settle that problem. I also wrote to the president of the C.P.R., but the authorities of that company do not want to hear about it. They say it would be too expensive, that, after all, the situation is not abnormal and that everything is going fine in Quebec city.
I suggested to the high ranking officials of the Department of Transport to go to Quebec city, to visit the places in question and to see the traffic jams caused when a train enters or leaves the station or when some shunting is done in the Canadian Pacific yards.
I reported all those facts to Mayor Hamel of Quebec city, who replied to me as follows:
I have just taken cognizance of your letter dated June 28 concerning level crossings in the city of Quebec. This important question has been our concern for many years.
I might say that in all our talks, we met considerable opposition, which explains why the question has not progressed further.
We shall renew our representations, in the hope that we may find a solution to this important problem.

Supply-Transport
I would therefore ask the minister to inquire in order to know who is responsible for this opposition met by the city of Quebec. Would it be the authorities of the Department of Transport, who do not care about it, or of the Canadian Pacific Railways, who refuse to listen to reason?
I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary who advocates the restoration of older Quebec to include in his projects an improvement of railway crossings.
I would also suggest to the minister to make some arrangements with the Canadian National Railways, the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway in order that the marshalling yard used by the C.P.R. may be demolished and transferred outside the walls of Quebec city perhaps to Ste Foy.
The C.N.R. advocates the construction of a passenger service station. They have a station at Ste Foy, since they already operate a service between Montreal and Quebec city, via the south shore, and they precisely stop at Ste Foy to leave passengers, and I think it would be more logical if that station was situated in the suburbs. Then the problem would be solved and, by the same token, the railway crossings, which are a public danger, would be eliminated. If the C.N.R. would develop outside of Quebec city a railway centre and a marshalling yard the problem would be solved.
I make that suggestion and I am convinced that the minister will make the required representations to the authorities concerned, so that we, the people in Quebec city, might also profit from downtown improvements and some day see the elimination of those notorious railway crossings which interfere with traffic.

I do not want to delay the committee unduly but I would like to express my surprise that the hon. member for Three Rivers criticized the monopoly situation that exists at airports across the country, because the agreements providing for this situation were concluded, I believe, while the previous government was in office, and when he was the minister responsible.
It is well known that the hon. member for York-Humber and I have raised this matter in the house, in connection with air terminal transport at Toronto international airport. It is now surprising to find an endorsement of our stand by the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I would like to thank him very
[Mr. Beaule.3
much for his support in our efforts to have this situation looked at again.
I wish to bring the minister's attention to the matter of express delivery in the suburbs of metropolitan Toronto. When I moved to Toronto a few years ago I was amazed to find that in the suburb of Scarborough prepaid express operated in the following manner. One day a truck appeared at my door and the driver demanded 75 cents a parcel for delivery of prepaid express articles. This seemed a rather strange situation so I went down to the express office to discuss it with the people there because I had not received notice that the shipment was coming to me.
I had no opportunity at all to pick it up myself, and I was quite surprised there was not free delivery by the express companies, C.N. and C.P., on this sort of service in such a large community as Scarborough which contains over 200,000 people.
Communities of much smaller size get free delivery service as part of the express service operated by the express companies. I am sure Scarborough is not the only suburb of Toronto which faces this problem, and I would ask the minister to have a look at it. I should like to relate briefly an experience I had in this connection some years ago. I had ordered some lobsters. I knew they were coming and called the express office repeatedly to find out whether this shipment had arrived. We had organized a dinner party at which we intended to serve the lobsters. We were expecting them on a certain day and I called the express office at 9.30 that morning and was informed that the lobsters had arrived. I said "Fine. I will come right down and pick them up." "Well," the fellow said to me on the telephone, "you cannot pick them up, they are already on the truck". I said "Isn't that rather strange? You fellows got a good start this morning." He assured me they were on the truck. By noon they had not arrived and he told me "Oh well, the truck takes a whole lot of these things; it goes on a circuitous route. But don't worry, it will be along". I called again at two o'clock, and finally at 6.30, by which time my wife was in a near state of panic, the lobsters arrived.
I am not suggesting there is collusion between the express officials and the local delivery service but a number of people have asked me why it is they are not informed that shipments have arrived, so that at least if they do not have an express delivery service they would have the option of picking them up on their own. I received two or

three letters recently in this connection from people pointing out that since they lived in such a populous area they should be given the same consideration as people in downtown Toronto or in other communities throughout Canada.
I find it difficult to defend the present policy, particularly since we were told that the marshalling yards which were built, despite considerable objection from people in certain parts of my constituency, would rationalize the whole railroad picture in Toronto. We were told: Just wait and see, and when these yards are in operation all the problems will be solved. Well, this is one problem which has not been solved and I hope the minister will get answers to some of the questions I have to ask on this matter. I should like to know why we are not given delivery service by the express company, a service which is given to much smaller communities as well as to other parts of metropolitan Toronto. I should like to know why under the present arrangements patrons are not informed of shipments having arrived, so that they can pick them up themselves. I have been told by the express people in the local office that this is impossible-that they cannot cope with this work. I say that if there is such a volume of business it should warrant the express company having a truck or trucks down there to take care of it. In the second place, I should like to know more about this arrangement between the railway and the local carrier-it is always the same carrier. Is this franchise -and it appears to be that-the result of tender or is it just some arrangement which is made by the railroads? If there is such an arrangement, are the railroads getting a "kick back" from this operation? These are the questions I should like the minister to inquire into. Certainly the people in my constituency would be most interested in knowing the answers.

In the few minutes remaining before five o'clock I want to introduce a new topic. It concerns grain handling facilities in the port of Vancouver. I had wished to make some lengthy remarks with regard to the development of the national harbours board facilities in the port of Vancouver, but perhaps I could leave these to a later occasion, perhaps later on during consideration of these estimates, or at some other time.

Delighted.
Supply-Transport

I am sure the minister will be delighted, as I can see from his expression. I wish to direct my observations now to the question of grain handling facilities in the port of Vancouver. The unprecedented wheat sales over the last year has meant the passage of some 200 million bushels of wheat through the port of Vancouver-more than Vancouver has ever shipped before. All the facilities of the port have been strained and put to the test in dealing with this record shipment. Vessels have stayed in the harbour sometimes for weeks on end awaiting berths. As a result there have been considerable losses to shipping companies. We do not have sufficient facilities to handle all the wheat which was offered at the port.
I wish to refer to an article which appeared in the New York Times on August 30, 1964 which sums up the wheat shipment story in these words:
Vancouver has been shipping 20 million bushels of grain a month during the year. There are 11 grain loading berths, but if the port facilities were better, a $500 million wheat transaction with Moscow might have been more than 10 per cent higher.
Full use of the berths handling 200 million bushels of wheat a year was pledged last year and, despite a promised expenditure of millions of dollars for increased facilities, ships still wait while costs mount.
There has been considerable discussion in Vancouver as to whether or not increased facilities should include an elevator or whether there should merely be an upgrading of existing grain handling facilities. A survey was made by the previous incumbent of the office of minister of transport. This survey took place toward the end of 1963 with a view to securing advice on what would be required by way of additional facilities at Vancouver and other ports of Canada. Since that time there have been rumours and stories in the Vancouver papers that private enterprise grain handling companies or co-operatives would be willing to build an elevator in the port of Vancouver to provide additional storage. So it seems to me we are coming close to a point where additional storage and grain handling facilities, rather than just working or handling facilities, should be developed in the port.
