The house resumed from Thursday, July 9, consideration of the motion (Mr. Orlikow):
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wonder if I may rise on a question of personal privilege. As hon. members will recall, I previously participated in the debate on this matter and on July 9 as reported on page 5259 of Hansard there is record of a question put to me by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. At that time the hon. member inquired whether a person whose reliability was questioned would have the right to appear before the security review board, and also whether he would have the right to appear with counsel. At that time I gave it as my understanding that he would have such a right. But in the discussions that have taken place-as hon. members opposite are aware -with the responsible officers, it has come to my attention that it is the British practice which is to be followed here, and there will be no right to appear personally or with counsel. The function of the review board is merely to review the file that already exists. I make this statement, Mr. Speaker, so that hon. members opposite will not be misled in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should start by saying, "As I was saying on July 9 at six o'clock". At that time I was dealing with a particular aspect of security matters and I had brought before the house the case of a young man who was working within a government department and applying for another position in the same department, but one which required a security clearance. The case was brought to my attention by the B.C. civil liberties association. The young man had refused to answer certain questions about his in-laws; he claimed
[The Chairman.]
this was information which he should not reasonably be expected to have. I should like to deal with that particular aspect of security matters for a few minutes.
It seems to me that a person should be judged upon his own character and background; that there should be sufficient opportunity from interview, from checking the records and references of a person, from speaking to his previous employers and those people who had something to do with his education and background generally, to find out what type of a person he is and whether he is a satisfactory security risk. In my opinion it is very unreasonable to check the status of a very large number of relatives and to reach any sort of conclusion about a person based upon such a check. A person from a large family might be at a very great disadvantage; he may have uncles, aunts and cousins who belong to various political parties and organizations, over whom he surely has no control. I think we presume that such people have too much influence upon an individual. I suggest that this type of question is unnecessary and there are adequate means of checking the individual without going into the case histories of all his relatives.
At the conclusion of my remarks when this matter was being debated previously, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned the case which was brought to the attention of the house last year by my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). This was the case of a young man who had been released from the Royal Canadian Navy because a security check revealed that his uncle had once been a communist. Of course, the error was found out; there was a confusion of names. The man whom the security officers thought was the young man's uncle was not his uncle at all, and the young man was given a security release. At that time I concluded my remarks by asking: "What if his uncle had been a communist?" This is a very unfair burden for such a young man to carry. He should be judged upon his own character, his own background, his own education, his own working record. I imagine this would be a particularly hard burden for some young people in this country who may be very orthodox and conform in every way, but whose parents may not conform and may be very radical. Are they to carry that burden throughout their lives?
We are dealing here with cases involving the careers of individuals. This is most important, Mr. Speaker. They should be judged

upon their own characters, and not upon those of their relatives, no matter how close those relatives may be.
On the general subject of security procedures, just before I rose to speak on July 9 the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) had been stoutly defending the government's position on security matters, and in particular the statement the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made on October 25, 1963. At that time I said:
The millennium in security procedures was not reached on October 25, 1963.
I pointed out that the millennium had not been reached on that date in this country, and still has not been. We do not consider the board of review which was established at that time to be satisfactory at all. As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) pointed out, this is not a judicial body. It is an administrative body, but it has quasi-judicial powers. It seems to me to be an altogether wrong principle for a body having judicial powers of any sort to be part of the general administrative set-up of the government. If it is to have judicial powers, it should be appointed as a judicial body. The type of persons appointed to judgeships is the sort we want, namely those appointed independently of the government.
As the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Macdonald) admitted a few moments ago, the present board of review does not permit the person under investigation to appear before it; he cannot be represented by counsel. This is a most unsatisfactory situation. Again I would reiterate that the careers of persons are being affected here, and their careers may be permanently affected by the wrong sort of security information. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, events in this country in the last month should give us cause for concern about the kind of people who are involved in our security investigations. I have an idea that they are not of the best and most reliable character. They can be given a great deal of wrong information, and may be supplying to the authorities wrong information upon which the authorities act in some cases, as they did in the case of the young man from Nanaimo, British Columbia, who was in the Royal Canadian Navy.
There is one other matter in connection with security that I would like to raise. I wonder whether any review has been carried out recently of the number of positions in the
Motions for Papers
federal government service of Canada who are subject to security checks. It seems to me that if you examined all the government departments, all the crown corporations and all the various crown agencies there would be a great many positions for which security checks are required. I believe they would number many thousands. I wonder whether this situation could not be examined to see if they are not carrying out security checks for far too many positions. It is my belief that the number of people working for the government of Canada who would have access to information that would be of any real value to an enemy would really be extremely small. I would suggest to the department that this sort of review should be undertaken so that we may keep to an absolute minimum the number of positions within the government with regard to which security checks are required.
I believe it was the hon. member for Greenwood, supported by the hon. member for Peace River, who suggested that perhaps a house committee should be established, to sit in camera, so that this question of security could be more fully explored by members of the house. Any time security matters have been raised in the house, ministers of justice of this country have seemed to become awfully sanctimonious and have thrown out the suggestion that the security of the nation is involved and they cannot answer any questions. I suggest that the members of the house at least have a right to know what are the procedures that are followed by the government. If it is felt that these matters should not be made public, and perhaps there is a good case to be put forward for that contention, this type of inquiry could be carried out by a house committee sitting in camera. Surely if we can have a committee meet in camera to discuss the flag, we can go into this very important subject which deals with the civil and individual liberties of Canadians. Therefore I again put the suggestion that this should be given consideration, because for our part we will not be satisfied until we know more of what is involved in the government's security policy.
I conclude my remarks by reminding hon. members that the security of the nation is very important certainly, but the liberties of individuals, their freedom and their right to a career is also important. We must not forget that, because we have by no means yet reached a happy balance between security and civil liberty in Canada.

Motions for Papers

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the last speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond (Mr. Prittie), in discussing this motion. I think there is a mystique among government circles or those in councils of state, so to speak, about secrecy and the ramifications of it. In fact, I think it is time we took a look at the whole problem. In France, as I understand it, with their system of the conseil d'etat, the citizen has such right if he is injuriously affected by a wrong ruling; we all remember the case of the young sailor which we discussed in the house last October. But there is no such right of action in this country, and I think it is time that we revamped our system and brought into our law a body of public law to protect the citizen.
I am thinking here of an article in the August 15 edition of The Economist in which the author was discussing the concept of the ombudsman and showing that really an ombudsman would not go far enough. To reinforce his argument he referred to the French system of the conseil d'etat and cited numerous examples, one of which might have been taken from our own Canadian experience as it concerned a young man in a department of government who, just because of rumour, had been dismissed. But in France this person had a right of action. He was reinstated by an order of the conseil d'etat and was also awarded damages.
I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond-and I know others have discussed this-has a point here and that we really should have a committee consider the matter. I am not worried about any proliferation of committees in this house if the committees have something interesting and really useful to do. I think we should go into this whole system.
In a little book called the "British Government Observed", Professor Brian Chapman of Manchester University makes some very useful comments in some 64 pages of his book. I do not know how one could possibly observe the British or any government in 64 pages, but he does it in a very interesting way. He discussed what I have called this mystique of secrecy. We all bow before the altar and say that everything is all right, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has said that all the procedures have been followed through and there is really no problem. This in a land of the free just is not good enough. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald) on a point of privilege said that everything was all right, that

there was a review board, that the person who is being charged really does not have to come and that he cannot have counsel. But I know that in his heart the parliamentary secretary deplores having to make such an admission in this house. I know him and I respect him, and I know you do not have to be a lawyer to have a conscience.
It is a lot easier if you have not.

Perhaps the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) has a point there.
I liked the reference in this article to the council of state for Britain, in which it was suggested that the council is really not the enemy of the administration but is its conscience. I think that an administration based on Liberal principles-we are going to be talking about this a great deal in another city in the next few days, and this will be bowing before the tenets of Liberalism-should be proud to say that this system of public law which they might bring about is their conscience and their guideline, instead of saying that the Prime Minister says everything is all right, do not butt in or bother finding out whether a man's rights are affected or not.
If the parliamentary secretary in his point of privilege had brought in a statute, then we could rejoice with him and think that this terrible problem is really being attended to. I am told that the United States state department even today, which must be ten years after the nefarious McCarthy-type inquiry was prevalent, has not recovered from the terrible damage done to it by the sort of loose, false and unsubstantiated charges which were made in those days. I am not drawing any parallel, thank heaven, on this aspect-and I want to be clear here-between the two countries, but it might happen here. It did happen in the United States. Last October we were given an example where it could happen to a small, modest person. But the fact that in Canada in 1964 a citizen has not the right to go before the board of review and has not the right to be confronted by his accuser, which seems to me to be the crux of the matter, as well as be confronted by the evidence-I hope I will be corrected if I am wrong about this- leads me to submit that it is time that the mighty Liberal party got into high gear and attended to the matter so that we could all approve of their action.
At the end of Dr. Brian Chapman's book there is a little statement which I am going

to share with the house because I think it cuts through the fog which seems to emanate from government benches whenever we get into matters affecting secrecy. He says:
This passion for secrecy has some constitutional support, but it clearly has much profounder psychological and sociological origins. Secrecy in public life panders to a craving for a sentiment of selfimportance, of belonging to an inner circle.
Here I admit that the author is discussing crown privilege and so on, but I am satisfied that there is a very clear parallel. It is all part of the same sort of mystique or fog. He goes on:
There is no doubt that this sentiment is frequently exploited in order to absorb critics and potential reformers into the system.
I think the government would do itself honour if it allowed this motion to pass and if the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) had the privilege of examining these documents. I think this precedent, which the government should readily accept, would go a long way toward clearing up a most unfortunate attitude among members of the general public to this very serious problem. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) said that no more important subject could be considered by a committee. I am not able to put matters in order of priority in this way, but I do think it would be well for this House of Commons if we could take really effective action to improve the security measures in this country and, at the very least, give a citizen the right to be confronted, as I said, by his accusers, to see the evidence and have counsel.
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in the very few minutes remaining before this debate must be interrupted, because of the regrettable absence at this point of my colleague for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who hopes to be here later but may not arrive in time to avail himself of the opportunity the rules provide to make a five minute reply at the end of the debate.
On his behalf however, and on behalf of all of us who are associated with him, I should like to say that we feel the debate that has taken place on this motion demonstrates very clearly that the motion should be allowed to pass. The request contained therein is for the tabling of a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations. For the reasons stated today by the 20220-516
Motions jor Papers
hon. member for Bumaby-Richmond, and for the reasons just now stated so well by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), it seems to me that all parts of this house would be true to their best traditions if they agreed to this motion.
If any statement made during the whole course of this debate clinches the argument, Mr. Speaker, I suggest it is the statement made this afternoon on a matter of privilege by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald). I will not make any extended observations on the fact that he was not sure of his ground when he spoke on July 9 during this debate, but I think there is tremendous significance in what he said today, namely that despite these new procedures set up by this Liberal government, including a board of review, these procedures that are supposed to protect the liberties and the rights of the individual, an admission is now made that the suspected individual does not have the chance to appear before the board of review. That being the case, it seems to us that the least the government should be willing to do is make public these statements and directives which, for all practical purposes, are laws of the land-laws under which people may lose their positions, or have their lives seriously affected for all time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is our hope that the government will change its mind with respect to the position stated earlier and agree to allow this motion to pass. If the government does not see fit we shall, of course, when the time comes, ask the house to vote on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I think the debate that has taken place so far in this house in respect of this notice of motion for the production of papers has been very useful in that it has drawn into focus some of the very real problems with which most members are familiar respecting this matter of investigating what are normally called national security risks. Whether this motion passes or not, we should like to know what the government is going to do about this board of review that was promised by a former minister of justice. Several months ago he promised, under great pressure I think, that this board of review was going to be set up. As has been stated this afternoon by the parliamentary secretary, and again by the previous speaker, there is now no possibility of an accused being able to present himself before this board of review and present his case directly. It seems to me that we have

Motions for Papers
lost some of the hope we had for justice being done in cases where serious mistakes have been made.
I should also like to say, Mr. Speaker, that in most of the democratic countries of the western world there have been adopted security risk procedures, if I may refer to them as such, that are almost indefensible when you try to reconcile them with the personal freedoms and personal rights of citizens. I am led to believe that in Australia and New Zealand they also have difficulty in carrying out what they consider to be proper investigations of these matters of national security risks. In spite of some measures that have been taken, such as the establishment of an ombudsman in New Zealand, this is still not completely satisfactory in so far as doing justice where mistakes have been made is concerned.
Some cases have been brought to the attention of this house where serious mistakes have been made, and this has been admitted. I am aware of other individual cases which have not been forcibly drawn to the attention of the house, in spite of the fact they have been referred to the Department of Justice on a number of occasions for re-examination. At this date I am still convinced that mistakes have been made, mistakes in so far as the conclusions that were reached on sloppy evidence, if I may use that word, gathered by the person doing the investigating.
Whether this motion passes or not, Mr. Speaker, surely on the basis of what the government has said from time to time, and on the basis of the sentiment expressed from many corners of this house, it ought to be willing to do something so that individuals who think they have been falsely accused will have some recourse, and that in this right to recourse they will have the opportunity of appearing before a board at which, if they are not confronted directly by the accusers, they ought to be faced with some of the so-called evidence against them. This is not an unreasonable request in my view, and although this relaxation may in some cases reveal the methods that are used by the investigating officers, surely this would be a small price to pay in relation to maintaining justice for those who have been falsely accused.
I do not intend to go into this situation further, or mention a lot of names and cases with which I personally am familiar and concerning which I believe justice has not been done, because to do so would initiate

other problems. I do hope however that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald), and his minister, will give some very serious consideration to allowing some sort of recourse by means of a board of review, or otherwise, so justice can be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply on the estimates of the Department of Transport. When the committee rose at five o'clock we were discussing vote No. 1.

Mr. Chairman, I ask the indulgence of the committee to complete the very few remarks that I had begun when five o'clock was called, on the subject ef grain handling facilities in the harbour of Vancouver. I think after the present season consideration must surely be seriously under way

Supply-Transport
with regard to the provision of an additional elevator in the port of Vancouver. That being so I would like to conclude with a few remarks regarding its placement.
The harbour of Vancouver, on the Vancouver side, is growing and becoming well filled with general cargo handling facilities. There is however ample space on the north side of the harbour for bulk handling facilities, and I think it would be the hope of many people who are familiar with that port that additional grain handling facilities be placed on that shore rather than on the Vancouver side. In making this suggestion I would point out that there is one difficulty which faces the construction of bulk handling facilities on the north side of Vancouver harbour, and that is access to that shore, because interswitching, as members familiar with the port know, is across the old second narrows bridge. This bridge is old and is coming to the end of its real usefulness.
I would suggest to the minister that in approaching this problem he and his engineers should give serious consideration again to an old, old idea; that is, to building a causeway across the neck of the north arm, which would cut off the flow of water into the north arm, control it with a lock, which would then permit rail movement from the north shore, across the causeway, across the north arm, through a tunnel in the mountain on the west side of the entrance to the north arm, and connect with the rail which now enters at the Imperial Oil plant at Port Moody on the Indian arm.
The effect would be to provide a circuit, or a horseshoe route on the Vancouver side of the harbour to the North Vancouver side; it would provide interswitching without the use of a bridge or a lift span; it would prevent the removal eventually of the existing old second narrows railway bridge, and it would do some other rather remarkable things. The flow of water into the harbour of Vancouver at Prospect point to the first narrows at peak runs is now at something in the neighbourhood of six knots, which makes it difficult for vessels moving in and out at peak flows. This however would cut off a considerable portion of the water which must flow into the harbour at high tide and it would indeed reduce considerably the flow of water at the first narrows and also at the Second narrows, where over the years there has been considerable difficulty in navigation while the tides are moving. Such a causeway would also create, of course, a fresh water body, which is a rather interesting thing. This
[Mr. Deachman.f
body would gradually convert itself to a fresh water body-I am referring to the waters of the north arm-and that would have considerable advantage indeed for log storage and other purposes. It would enable Vancouver to have a harbour railway which would run clean around the port of Vancouver, around the Indian arm to Port Moody and along the north shore without having to resort to the interswitching charges, which raise freight rates, back and forth between the north shore and the Vancouver side of the harbour. It would provide access for mainline railways coming down the Fraser valley to the north side of the harbour, which would be of very great advantage to that side of the harbour.
The whole project, if one looks at the map, consists of putting the fill into a narrow neck of water at the entrance to the north arm, the fill being provided from the tunnel which would have to be driven for about a mile through the mountain to connect with the rail at the Imperial Oil refinery at Port Moody. This would enable the use of the whole north shore of the harbour for the development of bulk loading facilities of all kinds.
There are new bulk loading wharves going up on the north shore. There is ample space there for the development of a grain elevator. I commend this project to the minister and his engineers for their careful study, before coming to any decision regarding the building of an elevator on that side, because this long term project would be of inestimable value in the total growth of the harbour of Vancouver.

Mr. Chairman, I feel obliged to say something on the Department of Transport estimates because I did not have the opportunity to do so last year. I also know something of the sensibilities and aspirations of the new minister and I know he would be annoyed if a maritimer did not say a few words about this important department. I intend only to mention general matters and two which have particular constituency application. The general subjects to which I wish to refer are winter navigation and the merchant navy, which are old favourites of mine. I am not going to go into their past history; I just want to emphasize one or two points which have come up and perhaps bring the committee up to date. I may mention from time to time in my remarks the Atlantic development board, but it will be with reference to genuine transportation matters. For proof of the importance of transport to the

maritimes one has only to consider the fact that many, if not most of the subjects with which the Atlantic development board are dealing concern transportation matters.
With regard to winter navigation hon. members will recall that the Atlantic development board made a thorough review of the effects of icebreaking in the St. Lawrence on the ports of Saint John and Halifax. They made a very good survey and a press release was published in this regard. There are also other surveys being conducted with respect to Saint John and Halifax. I remember that at the time the survey was referred to them there were some misgivings that the board might be involving themselves in activities not within their compass, but I think that this particular survey has proved to be a very good type of reference for them. In view of some of the activities in which the board are engaging I think it is worthy of note that this survey has met with the approval of everybody.
I should like to refer to two matters in the report which was published, this being my first opportunity to do so. If I may quote directly from the press release of the Atlantic development board dated May 15 of this year regarding winter navigation in the St. Lawrence river and gulf as it affects the Atlantic ports, it is significant to note that this was said:
The main weight of the loss referred to falls upon Saint John, reflecting partly the greater volume of general cargo transshipment traffic through that port.
Everyone knows that it is the loss of general cargo about which we are concerned. I will not labour that particular point because it has been already debated, but on page two of the same press release a statement appears which I should like to put on record. I do not think this is an attempt to rewrite history in which the minister may have been involved, but the board make this statement:
In the winter of 1957-58 the federal government began to provide icebreaker assistance to vessels entering the gulf.
Every schoolboy knows that this icebreaking activity was going on long before that, so I do not know why the year 1957-58 was mentioned particularly. Perhaps it was selected arbitrarily.
I recall that when I first came to the house in 1953 I made a speech, and if anyone would care to look it up they would find it dealt specifically with icebreaking activity at that particular time, about which I was complaining. This report of the board is an example
Supply-Transport
of their work and is very comprehensive, but we still have not reached a solution. I presented a brief to the board in Saint John. When I did so I think they felt that I might have been adopting a partisan approach, but the board were very cordial to me. The two points I wanted them to consider, and which I mention now because of their significance to this department, were these. I think the federal government should admit fully their responsibility to Saint John and Halifax, promises to this effect having been made ever since confederation. Second-and this is more from the point of view of the public relations of the department-the government should make public exactly what they are doing in the St. Lawrence so far as icebreaking is concerned. There is no sense in trying to hide this. If they do make their activities known I think the sort of controversies which occur each fall might be avoided.
With respect to the merchant navy, hon. members will recall that I have raised this subject for many years now. In a private member's motion this year I pointed out that there was a greater need than ever for the revival and development of a Canadian merchant marine. I showed that men would be trained for the sea and there would be a tremendous help from a defence standpoint. I also mentioned that with the increasing development of bulk cargo throughout the world it is even more important from this trade point of view that Canada have its own ships. Today the S.I.U. seem to be making moves, with elections coming up shortly, to bring about perhaps a more stable future for seamen. However, a certain matter was called to my attention which indicates the state of mind still existing in Canada, and which the minister will have to overcome if he sincerely hopes to do something about the merchant navy.
On August 6 last I asked a question in the house of the minister of external affairs with respect to the United Nations conference on trade and development which took place in March of this year in Geneva. The resolution on which I based my question was framed in this way:
All countries should co-operate in devising measures to help developing countries to build up maritime and other means of transport for their economic development to ensure the unhindered use of international transport facilities.
The surprising thing, Mr. Chairman, when this resolution was put to the meeting, was that Canada abstained. There were 92 in favour, 7 against with 17 abstentions. We stated why Canada was against the resolution,

Supply-Transport
and I suppose I should mention the reason. It was because we felt that the special principles should make it clear that the building up of maritime transport in developing countries should be based on sound economic criteria.
Although this may seem obscure, Mr. Chairman, I mention it to show the state of mind existing in Canada which the minister will have to overcome in order to make us more sea conscious. We are basically a nation of landlubbers. I just mention this to spur the minister on. Mr. Chairman, I mentioned the two general matters, winter navigation and revival of the merchant marine. I should now like to discuss two local problems in my constituency. The minister did not make a statement at the beginning of our consideration of his estimates. I do not seriously object, because I think we would really be perpetuating the bad habit we have acquired in referring to minor items on the discussion of first item. Actually such details should be referred to at a later time during our discussion of particular items. However having received the invitation to do so, I intend to mention these two local matters.
At the outset I should like to state that in discussing these items I have an opportunity to pay tribute to a distinguished marine agent in Saint John who died very suddenly last week. He was a very devoted civil servant and at all hours 'of the day could be called on to deal with the many problems which were brought to him. I refer to the late Frank A. McKinnon.
First, we have one of the few municipal airports left in Canada in Saint John. It is a good airport of which we are proud, and we are pleased that we have been able, in a private enterprise way to survive. I have heard a great deal of talk on numerous occasions about this airport being sold to the federal government, although that idea is not mine. I hope that if serious negotiations ever take place the federal government will make a very handsome offer to the municipal authorities.
We have experienced problems, and I do not say that any particular favour has been played by the federal government in respect of other airports with which we are in competition, but it seems impossible, with its importance and the growing demands for new improvements, to compete with other completely federally operated airports. Recently in Saint John v/e have had difficulty as a result of weather conditions, and a lot of flights have been cancelled. Hon. members know that there is no such thing as a fog

in Saint John, or we never admit this publicly, but many flights have been cancelled recently. I think public relations on the part of the government have fallen into a bad state.
I suggest a weather forecaster should be appointed for the Saint John airport under the Department of Transport. Our weather forecasts now originate in Halifax and are accurate for the most part, and probably serve a purpose, but I suggest to the minister that a weather forecaster be appointed for the Saint John area in order to dispel criticism that falls on the government whenever a flight is cancelled. I think such a man could be a very useful buffer between the public and the government, putting an end to the criticism that, whenever a flight is cancelled in Saint John at the same time flights are operating out of Fredericton, Moncton and Halifax, it is the fault of the government. I am not complaining because flights have been cancelled, but suggest that from a public relations standpoint, if for no other reason, the minister would be justified in seriously considering some sort of an employee with sole responsibility for deciding whether or not flights should be cancelled.
The second matter of local interest to which I should like to refer is a harbour bridge. A day or two ago, I asked the Minister of Transport a question about the Atlantic development board and its consideration in respect of assistance toward the development of a harbour bridge in Saint John. I do not intend to deal with this subject at any length, and I should have liked to include Halifax in my remarks, but there has been some criticism in this regard. I agree to a certain extent that the Atlantic development board should not be involved in this type of activity, but the field is now wide open. The board is assisting in the building of roads and other things, and I think this is about the only way we in Saint John are going to be able to afford such a bridge. Therefore, it seems the Minister of Transport is going to be responsible in some way for dealing with this problem. I hope that he will consider this idea favourably, and provide some assistance through the Atlantic development board, or the national harbours board -which would be involved if the bridge was built in a certain location in the harbour- or perhaps through the municipal loans board.
I should like to make two comments in conclusion, Mr. Chairman. I was pleased to hear the minister announce that there would be further grants in lieu of taxes in con-

nection with the national harbours board property. This will be welcomed by all the national ports affected. I also noted that St. John's, Newfoundland, is to be included as a national harbours board port, and we think this is good, and are very pleased. I suppose one could say there really is not much competition between Saint John, New Brunswick, and St. John's, Newfoundland, but by such an inclusion of the national ports, a tradition is maintained.
I should like to say in connection with the national harbours board that I have always felt it to be a very good agency. From time to time criticism has been levelled at the board but it has always done a good job and I hope plans go forward for protecting its future. Often we hear the suggestion that in this day and age serious changes might have to be made, but the board agency in Saint John has been very helpful to our port.
The previous member who spoke, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, referred to the grain elevators in Vancouver. We have two or three grain elevators in Saint John, but the grain elevator which was operated by the Canadian National Railways became little used and in bad repair, and there is now a suggestion that it should be sold. I think that the national harbours board, which has had tremendous success in the operation of grain elevators, should take over this elevator in Saint John on a permanent basis. I refer, of course, to that elevator in the centre of the city.
One other matter I wish to mention, and I am not going to do so in great detail tonight, is the Maritime Freight Rates Act and related problems. I understand the suggestion has been put forward by the hon. member for Peace River and others, that it is advisable that in respect of any piece of legislation which comes forward as a result of the MacPherson report, there should be some method of segregating the discussions. I am interested in railway legislation that affects the maritimes and am less concerned at the moment with railway abandonment, which looms so large out west. But, I think if there were special subcommittee groups to deal with each aspect of this type of legislation they would be of tremendous help to the minister and those who are going to be affected.
I have dealt with two national matters, the first being winter navigation, and I am sure that the subjects will be discussed again this fall. I hope the minister takes some of my advice in this regard. I tried to bring my
Supply-Transport
thinking in respect of the merchant navy up to date for the purposes of this debate, and I hope I have done so. I concluded my remarks by referring to two local matters which I hope the minister will consider. I deliberately did not prepare an address for this evening because I just wanted to mention these matters in a general way.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I have two matters I should like to discuss briefly now. As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert stated, these are local problems. I may enlarge upon them and give more details when we come to the particular items, namely the grade crossing fund and air services. In case we do not reach these items tonight, I want to refer now to the two problems that are of great interest to my home city of Moose Jaw. By my referring to them now, the minister might be in a position to give answers to these questions when we come to the particular items.
Dealing with the grade crossing fund first, I want to draw to the attention of the minister the protracted negotiations with the board of transport commissioners in regard to the plans drawn up by Moose Jaw to reduce the traffic hazard on what is called the Fourth avenue bridge over the main line, and the large freight yard of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am given to understand that officials of the board of transport commissioners have inspected the proposed renovations and changes to the overpass, and that they have agreed that these changes will greatly reduce the traffic hazard on the structure, which was designed for much slower traffic than the present flow of cars, trucks and buses, which at peak loads now form an almost continuous movement. The traffic hazard is particularly acute in winter because of snow and ice conditions.
I am sure the board of transport commissioners are impressed with the need for the proposed changes in the interest of greater safety and less traffic congestion. As a result of a telephone call home today I was informed by city officials that full inspections and inquiries have been made by the board officials. If an early and favourable decision could be given it might be possible to arrange for some winter works on the project. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that he may help in having an announcement by the board of transport commissioners speeded up.

Supply-Transport
My other point, Mr. Chairman, relates to a press release from the Department of Transport dated August 18, and which is headed, "D.O.T. co-sponsors community airport planning research". This press release reads in part as follows:
The federal Department of Transport, in cooperation with the social science research council of Canada (a non-government, non-profit organization), is providing technical and financial assistance for a series of studies on what constitutes a good, economic community airport to serve the needs of training, recreational, local and itinerant flying. Dr. Neil McArthur associate professor of geography at the Royal Military College, Kingston, is conducting the studies.
Farther down the press release reads:
For the past two years Dr. McArthur has been doing research in the general field of community airport development in peninsular Ontario and in the integrating of small airports with the economic and recreation areas they serve.
I am speaking in the interests of my home city, Mr. Chairman. As the minister knows, Moose Jaw has a large R.C.A.F. station for pilot training on the new Tudor jets. There is also a small civilian landing field north of the city. There is no regular air service. I know there can be no commercial air flights from the R.C.A.F. base. I am speaking with regard to the possibility of extending the civilian airfield north of the city or the possibility of constructing a new landing field.
The previous government had a program for what were called local airstrips and development airstrips. In the case of development airstrips there was a federal grant of up to $100,000 for an approved project. In a statement issued in 1958 the minister of transport in the previous government referred to these development and local airstrips. His statement reads in part as follows:
In addition, there have been a great many cases recently where local authorities would like to have an airstrip as a means of improving the status of the municipality. These are not cases where schedule service is involved or where the existence of the air strip is essential to the community because of its remote location. They are cases in which the existence of an airstrip would appear desirable and helpful, although not essential, and where the strip would primarily be of benefit to the persons engaged in flying training, private flying, charter flying with small aircraft, and private business flying.
These projects do not fall in the essential category, but if on examination we determine that there is some possibility of use for these purposes that merits assistance, we will share in the total cost of this sort of project with an appropriate local entity, up to a maximum of $100,000 on the part of the federal government, with the local interest being allowed to include cost of the land
[Mr. Pascoe.I
in its share of the project. In these cases as well, title of the land would have to be transferred to the federal government, with the local authority assuming operational responsibility for the strip after construction.
I should like the minister to tell me if this program of federal assistance is still in force. As I said, Mr. Chairman, these remarks might have been held over until we reach item 30 for air services or item 82 for the grade crossing fund. I have made these brief references now so the minister will be in a position to answer when the items are reached. I trust he will be able to give me some information concerning these matters I have raised.

Mr. Chairman, I shall confine myself to questions at this point and not go into a lengthy speech. Perhaps the minister will answer my questions when the particular items are under discussion.
The first question I have is, have we rules and regulations covering pilots of all craft flying? For example do we have two pilots on all licensed airplanes, or where is the cut-off point? I should like to know this, and I should like to know also how long a pilot is allowed to fly a plane continuously before someone else takes over. In other words, what is his period of duty? I should like to know how often these pilots are called in for a medical check-up. I think this is very important in view of a statement made the other day at a medical meeting by a well regarded medical man to the effect that after 40 years of age two out of three of us are prone to coronary attacks. I am wondering if we should not look a little more closely at the rules and regulations in view of the vast expansion in flying.
A further question has to do with elevators. Is it the policy of the government to give a private elevator in business in a rival company the same service from the department as is given for example a C.N.R. elevator?
Then there is a further question I would like to ask the minister, and it has to do with low water levels, and this would involve northern affairs and public works, as well as transport. Would it be possible to take a rather more generous attitude where dredging must be done, due to low water levels, until this situation is controlled, either by dams or possibly by damming up tributaries to the great lakes? I would ask the minister to take a long look at this.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take a few moments of the time of the house, so

the minister can answer questions which are of particular concern to my constituency and especially to the town of St. Hyacinthe.
It is a well-known fact that, since 1957, St. Hyacinthe has been experiencing a remarkable development.
People who know something of this town located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river are aware that it is cut in two by C.N.R. tracks.
Several years ago, there were three roads one could take to get from what is known as the southern part of town to the northern section. Around 1940, if I remember correctly, two of those level crossings of access were closed, to be replaced by a tunnel for motor and horse-drawn vehicle traffic, at La-framboise boulevard.
This sufficed for a number of years, but as I said earlier, because of a large increase in population these last few years, it has become necessary to open at least another roadway, a tunnel, if you like, so as to make it easier to cross from one part of the city to the other.
At peak hours, at noon for instance, traffic is so heavy that workers are greatly delayed, since most factories are located on the north side of the railroad tracks.
I know that the St. Hyacinthe city council intends to ask for the construction of a tunnel off Choquette boulevard. I would not be surprised if negotiations were already under way with government representatives. I should like to take this opportunity to ask the minister to give his kind attention to the requests submitted to him or to any division of his department. This matter is of capital importance.
By using his influence, not only will the minister have done a lot to gain the esteem of the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot in the House of Commons but I know that the population of the city of St. Hyacinthe will be grateful to him. His kindness and his graciousness will have won him their affection.
I would not want to deprive him of the opportunity to make a name for himself.
That is why I urge him to give special consideration to that request when the city council gets in touch with him.

I had not intended to speak at length on the estimates of the Department of Transport, and my intention was based on two reasons which I shall explain later. However, since the minister's opening statement was reduced to an invitation to members of the
Supply-Transport
committee to make suggestions to him on what he ought to talk about, I feel compelled to take part in the discussion and to invite him to address himself to certain specified matters.
It seems to me there is a certain amount of overlapping between the discussion now taking place and the debate on Bill No. C-120. That bill is of such magnitude and complexity that it covers a large part of the activities of the department. I do not want to discuss, its provisions but I would like to make a few suggestions, which I hope the minister will support, on how the bill should be proceeded with from this point forward. We should recognize that it may be preferable: to send the bill to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines at an earlier stage than is ordinarily done. The reason I suggest this is because after second reading and agreement in principle it may be more difficult to accept amendments suggested by the committee.
I also suggest that there may be profound differences of opinion respecting certain clauses in the bill and, if they are agreed to in principle on second reading before representation is made on them in the committee, it may make matters more difficult.
Further I would ask for the minister's cooperation in reorganizing the committee structure of the house to some extent, to meet the need we will face with respect to the railways bill. The committee may find it necessary to break up into subcommittees to consider various aspects of the legislation, and there are at least three major aspects of it that should be considered separately. Also there should be an extension of the life of the committee beyond prorogation, and when I talk about prorogation I have in the back of my mind some date just before Christmas. Whether I am making a good guess or a bad one is immaterial, but if members on both sides have such a target date for prorogation it will be very difficult to finish consideration of the bill and have the committee's recommendations brought back to the house before then.
