1964 is the one I had in mind. I would not like to see all the work of the committee die at prorogation. I know that in 1945 and other years we got around this problem by simply adjourning rather than proroguing, so that the committees could carry on. But it seems to me we could do something now to give formal status to com-

Supply-Transport
mittees between sessions, so that there will be no need to use subterfuges of one kind or another. I hope the minister will give a favourable response-

I wonder whether the hon. member does not feel he should be addressing his appeal to his hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre who is, I understand, the chairman of a subcommittee on procedure which, as far as I can see, has proceeded at the slowest pace of any committee we have ever had.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I wonder whether I could be permitted to bring the Minister of Transport up to date. The committee on organization and procedure has set up a fourth subcommittee of which the hon. member for Medicine Hat is chairman. It is really a committee on committees, and what my hon. friend is doing is putting in a commercial on behalf of the good work of that committee.

At the beginning of his speech the hon. member for Medicine Hat said he would make some unorthodox remarks because I had issued an invitation for members to do so. Well, it was not an invitation; it was resignation. I do not mean that in a political sense, but in a philosophical sense. I was aware that a certain number of speeches would be made but I would not like to think that any member of this committee would be tempted to follow the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I think it would be wonderful if we could get through the general part of this discussion and turn to the detail as soon as possible. I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but I hope we will not get into a discussion here on the structure of special, sessional or standing committees of the house because that would lead us far astray. Nevertheless I am much interested in what the hon. gentleman says and I would like to talk to him about it behind the curtains.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That would ruin his plans.

I can assure the Minister of Transport that the work of the committee on organization and procedure and of the fourth subcommittee which deals with committee structure is proceeding as rapidly as possible. Some suggestions will be brought forward and we do need a favourable response from the Minister of Transport. I may add that they would assist him in getting his bill through parliament. It is not my purpose, however, to transgress the rules of the house

by discussing this matter any further. I have only brought it up because this is particularly applicable to the Department of Transport.
One question I should like the minister to discuss-and here again we are in the grey area where it is difficult to know whether or not one is transgressing the rules of order -concerns federal responsibility in the field of highway transport. This is a subject which has been brought up on a number of occasions. So far, it appears that the limited responsibility which the federal government has assumed has been exercised through the Department of Public Works. It seems to me that the growth in importance of highway transport in Canada indicates that it should properly belong to the Department of Transport. It is not good enough simply to transfer responsibility to the Department of Transport unless there is to be increased activity. If responsibility were transferred, we would assume the federal government would undertake a greater degree of responsibility. I believe that some of the expenditure proposed out of the railway rationalization fund, as I think it is called, could be better invested in improving highway transport than in keeping some of the uneconomic branch lines going over a long period of time when we know full well that some of them will be of diminishing value.
Another matter I invite the minister to discuss is this question of regional air line services. We have waited several months for a statement by the minister respecting a new policy on regional or feeder air line services. We have had a sad experience with what used to be called the southern prairie run. I want to tell the minister now that we do not want any repetition of what happened in connection with that service-the transferring of half a million dollars worth of equipment to TransAir under certain agreements, with the contracts left open to the point where TransAir, in this case, could renege on its responsibility to provide an air line service while keeping the $500,000 worth of equipment which was given to it.
We set up Trans-Canada Air Lines, now known as Air Canada, so as to provide air services for this country. It was not confined to providing air services from Vancouver to Toronto and Montreal, skipping over all the other cities in Canada without providing feeder or branch line services at all. If the trend which has been established continues, Air Canada will be telling us they have no aircraft smaller than the Viscount, which is a 60 passenger plane. It will then be

argued that no service can be provided to any city where traffic does not allow a reasonable load for a 60 passenger plane. It can be assumed that the Viscounts will be phased out in the course of the next three to five years and then we shall be in a position where Air Canada does not possess any aircraft smaller than the Vanguard. Where do we go from there?-to the DC-8? Would it reach a point where Air Canada has only DC-8 and DC-9 aircraft? These are not aircraft which can provide a satisfactory air service for Canada to include all our cities, and I think it is the responsibility of Air Canada to reconsider its policy in this respect. I do not accept the contention that Air Canada cannot own any aircraft smaller than a Viscount. There are all kinds of modern aircraft smaller than the Viscount which could be used to give a satisfactory and profitable air service to some of the smaller cities of Canada.
Medicine Hat, which I represent is not the only city to be affected. Swift Current, Yorkton, and other cities in Manitoba are affected. We are now without an air line service completely. Trans-Canada Air Lines withdrew over a year ago. TransAir then assumed the responsibility to provide this service but before a year had elapsed they withdrew. I am not suggesting the company should have continued the kind of air service it was providing. Representations were made time and again that its schedules were not conducive to attracting business. But instead of adjusting those schedules so as to make satisfactory connections with the transcontinental run the company simply produced figures illustrating its contention that the service was not being used to a sufficient level, and then withdrew.
I do not think it is valid to put forward the argument that profit or loss in connection with an air line service should be calculated between every point of landing. For example, the service between Calgary and Regina should not be calculated in such a way that it has to show a profit, any more than it should from Medicine Hat to Calgary, or from Toronto to Timmins, or between any other two points.
I think we have a right to expect reasonably comprehensive service for the whole country, and that the whole operation should be considered in the profit and loss statement. Certainly these feeder lines which feed into the transcontinental runs do not always pay for themselves because of their limited scale; but they do provide additional passenger and
Supply-Transport
freight loads for the long runs. Therefore I would ask the Minister of Transport to address himself to some of the questions I have raised, without asking him to duplicate the debate that is going to take place when the railway bill comes before the house. That bill may not come back to the house for several weeks, and we would like to have some direction as to its process through the committee before it comes back to the house and becomes law.

Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing item 1 of these estimates there are two matters I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister. The first concerns the general radio service, which is the name of the organization in Canada. In the United States, where the idea first originated, it is known as the citizens' band-the frequency band set aside for the use of citizens for general communications. I have here a letter I received from one of my constituents who belongs to the organization in Canada and points out the very inhospitable manner in which this government treats United States visitors when they bring this type of equipment into Canada. This letter reads in part as follows:
I am taking the liberty of enclosing our general radio service paper. (We) got two of these radios for business last spring and we have found them so helpful businesswise and pleasurewise. The Department of Transport apparently doesn't wish to recognize these radios or the clubs formed so that members are aware of all rules and regulations and realize the advantage of using our radios properly.
When their United States counterparts come to Canada-that is, the counterparts of the general radio service people in Canada-they are forced at the border point by our Canadian customs officials to shut off their transmission equipment, and I am told that in most cases this equipment is sealed so that it cannot be used while they are in Canada. These people call themselves CBers, and they have sent me their periodical in which appears an editorial headed "Let's Tear Down the Iron Curtain". I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the reference there is to the curtain of silence that is enforced by our laws in connection with visitors to this country. The editorial says:
Many CBers from the United States are arriving at our border expecting to travel into Canada for a vacation and visit with GRS operators in Canada on their travels. Unfortunately many of these tourists are being given a sour taste of Canadian government hospitality by having their CB sets sealed to prevent their use while in our country.

Supply-Transport
This editorial runs the length of the page and I will not burden hon. members by reading any more of it, but that is the gist of the editorial. I believe this periodical has a wide circulation. Elsewhere in this publication they give us some bad publicity in a section headed, "Welcome to Canada!" It is said, underneath a picture showing some of their radio equipment:
Here's the welcome greeting CBers from the United States get from the Canadian government when they arrive at the Canadian border. A customs seal is placed on their set in some way as to prevent any transmissions from the rig. In this case the mike was removed from the input and a seal placed on it so it could not be used without being broken. Through lack of an agreement, U.S. mobiles are not allowed to use the CB sets while in Canada. Consequently, a fortune in tourist business is lost each year from CBers who would come to visit and vacation in Canada if it was made legal for them to use their sets.
I am not raising this matter solely on behalf of United States citizens, no matter how worthy may be their motives. We know they bring a great many tourist dollars to our country, and we need this money and their business very badly. But that is not my reason for bringing this matter to the attention of the minister. I am speaking mainly for their Canadian counterparts who are not in such great numbers as is the case in the United States, but who form the general radio service club of Canada. I believe it is time the Canadian and United States governments entered into an agreement with regard to the common use of a radio band by these two allied organizations. Technically it could be the same band as that used in the United States. Agreement should be reached with regard to Canadian and United States communal use of this system. Our country is larger than the United States, and less populous. We could encourage the use of this facility in a manner commensurate with the encouragement it receives from our more populated neighbour country to the south.
I have been informed that this hobby, or operation-it is not completely a hobby; it is also for public use-is very popular amongst ranchers, forestry workers, lumbermen, the construction industry, missionary and social welfare workers in remote areas, and hobbyists in radio communications. I bring this matter to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, hoping that some effort will be made by the minister to correct this unfair situation.
Finally, I have received a communication from the international brotherhood of teamsters, chauffeurs, warehousemen, and help-

ers. This concerns, of course, the Canadian government railway. It is a protest against the continual escalation of subsidies to the Canadian government railway. You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that I did not say "Canadian National Railways"; I used the old term that was used when they were first founded, namely Canadian government railway. No matter how large an organization they have built up since then, we are responsible for the situation that exists in the railway. The letter is addressed to me and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
There is a very persistent rumour that the federal government has ordered various transport companies to use the piggyback services provided by Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railway companies in order to reduce the operating deficit of the railways. If there is any basis in fact for this rumour, then I strenuously object to the order, as this is unfair competition and displaces hundreds of men in the transport industry who would otherwise be moving these loads over the highways.
If the government of Canada is sincerely concerned in the displacement of men through automation, then I suggest that they consider the abolishment of piggyback orders, if they exist. The railways cannot possibly suffer by providing this service, as there is certainly not rate cutting that will be a benefit to the transport companies involved.
Further, the railways are continually buying out transport companies, or controlling shares in them, and are also cutting rates to the point where no tf-ansport company could possibly compete, and then when they experience an operating deficit they apply to the federal government for a subsidy. They are allowed to continue this rate cutting, and nothing is being done to curtail this practice. If a transport company operated in such a manner, where can they get a comparable subsidy?
There is no indication that the subsidy paid to the railways is not being applied to the transport companies they now control, and if this situation is allowed to continue, the economy of the country cannot possibly survive without additional tax burdens.
As a taxpayer of this country, I strongly resent the foregoing situation and suggest that all these points be thoroughly investigated and the populace of this country be informed of the true facts.
Submitted for the consideration and investigation of the respected house.
Yours truly,
R. Carron, President
That letter, Mr. Chairman, is from the international brotherhood of teamsters, chauffeurs, warehousemen and helpers and is sent from their local office in Kingston. In passing this letter on for the due and thorough consideration of the Minister of Transport and his department I would point out to the minister that there is a good deal of basic common sense in the letter.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very few words to say on the first item of the

estimates. I believe some months ago I made reference to the question of a national air policy and asked when the government would be bringing such a policy forward. It was stated on that occasion, I think, that the former minister, who is now President of the Privy Council, had had his officials study the question and that a new policy would be forthcoming some time in the future. I would like to impress on the minister and on the government the importance of that aspect to our economy today. Without in any way trying to detract from the good work the Minister of Transport is trying to do today, I think we can say that his department is loaded down quite heavily, particularly when one considers the fact that in the next two or three years the government will have before it the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation, and in particular the problems of railways. This will require a great deal of attention from the minister.
I believe there is a growing feeling in the country today that what we need in parliament is a minister for aircraft services and development. If we take a look at the increasing traffic on our highways, the increasing value of the civil aviation industry and the need for volume in the manufacturing of small aircraft, all of these matters indicate that this is a branch of government which needs more attention than it can possibly receive at the present time under one ministry, which has all the other transportation services under its jurisdiction. I want to leave that thought with the government, and I believe the minister has on one or two occasions voiced an opinion somewhat along the same lines.
However I do have a suggestion to offer. I am not too sure how practical it is, but it might be an indication of the increasing importance of civil aviation in this country. I would ask the minister whether some study will be given to the possibility of assisting glider clubs across the country as a means of eventually promoting an interest in smaller aircraft. I should also like to bring to the minister's attention, as I did on a former occasion, the fact that many of the people in our smaller towns are wondering whether the federal government and the Department of Transport are going to formulate a policy of assistance in the construction of local airports for smaller aircraft, the use of which no doubt in the next 40 or 50 years will become more frequent each year.
Another matter I want to raise concerns the port of Churchill. I am wondering whether
Supply-Transport
the minister can tell us whether there is any research being undertaken in order to try to stretch out the navigation season for that port.
The final matter I want to mention is with regard to the royal commission on transportation. I do not intend to go into this question in detail as we will have other occasions to discuss it, but I believe it is a very important matter which will be engaging our attention. Not only will the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines be considering it but I suggest subcommittees should also study various aspects of the matter as well, so that the whole question can be dealt with more expeditiously than would otherwise be the case. The minister's statement the other day left me a little disturbed, I must say, particularly his observations on the subsidy for passenger services. There were other matters mentioned which appeared to indicate that there might be some erosion of the Crowsnest pass rates. I know the minister will assure us that that is not the thought in mind, and I am not going to raise that particular aspect tonight.
There is one matter which, in view of the intentions of the railways to abandon some of the lines, might merit some consideration by the government, and it is the feasibility or necessity or possibility of providing some kind of bridge building incentive to the provinces in order to alleviate some of the hardships which might otherwse be caused by some of the rail line abandonments which seem, as far as the economy is concerned, to be soundly based. I do not think there is anything else with which I need deal at this particular time, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, whether or not we get the first item of these estimates through tonight, I hope the minister will take the floor. A good many things have been put to him about which he should make a comment or two, and I should like to emphasize two subjects concerning which it would be desirable to have a statement from him tonight. One is of pretty wide general application and the other affects a particular group of people.
I notice the minister pointing to the clock and that seems to be a suggestion that I co-operate so that he can get the floor. I assure him that I shall do so.
The first subject I want to underline has been dealt with or alluded to by a number of speakers, namely the question of a clear statement on the part of the government so far as air policy is concerned. I remind the minister that once, but only once in the

Supply-Transport
history of this country has there been a clear statement of government policy with respect to civil aviation. He knows when that was made and that I was a member of the house at the time. He was something more; he was a grey eminence.
I was not as grey then as I am now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Nor as eminent, either.
I refer to the civil aviation policy for the post-war period announced in this house in 1944 by Right Hon. C. D. Howe.
I think the hon. gentleman is rather mistaken. The policy was originally announced by Mr. Mackenzie King some months before that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That is right, Mr. Chairman, the general lines were first announced by the then prime minister, but a few months later, in 1944, Mr. Howe in a very clear and detailed statement gave us the full program, and it was clear and definite. This was one of those occasions when the members of the group to which I belong gave wholehearted support to that policy. I regret to say that within two years Mr. Howe started to whittle away at his own policy.
I see the Minister of Transport shaking his head but I can give him chapter and verse if he wishes. He does not want me to take the time, and accedes to my assertion that in 1946 Mr. Howe started to whittle away at that policy by changes that were made with respect to the question as to whether or not surface transportation companies could own air lines. Perhaps that is enough to convince the minister that I know whereof I speak.
From then we have gone on to still further watering down of the air policy set out by Mr. King and Mr. Howe in 194.4. At the present time, along with all the other dilutions of policy that have taken place both under the previous Liberal government and the previous Conservative government, we are now left with considerable uncertainty. The minister tells us that statements are going to be made, but we are kept waiting for them. In the meantime we are presented with rumours and press reports about some companies like TransAir wanting more deals, such as the hon. member for Medicine Hat and others have referred to tonight. This has been very unsatisfactory. I want to support the line that was taken by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, which is the line we have taken through the years, that the main cornerstone of aviation policy in this country should be Air

Canada. That was the heart of Mr. King's and Mr. Howe's policy of 1944, and we regret very much that governments that have been in power since have moved away from that policy.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am ready to cooperate and make it possible for the minister to make a statement tonight, so I need not spell this out. I just hope I have drawn his attention to it sufficiently, and that I have provoked him sufficiently, that he will say something clear and definite on this question tonight.
Mr. Chairman, I now turn to the other subject that is on my mind, and if I have not been sufficiently provocative with respect to civil aviation policy I will try a little harder now. I want to say something about the position of retired C.N.R. employees whose retirement took place before recent improvements were made in the pension plan of the C.N.R. I say to the Minister of Transport, my friend of his former Winnipeg days, that he is the biggest disappointment we have had in the ministry of transport with respect to this subject. Other ministers have at least promised to look into the matter themselves, but all this minister has done is to act as a messenger boy and refer the matter to Mr. Donald Gordon, and then refer us to what Mr. Donald Gordon has said.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this whole question of the position of retired people on pensions which were fixed in previous years or previous decades is one of national policy, and that the government has to be concerned not only about plans like the Canada pension plan, which we hope we will get some day, but about retired civil servants, other groups such as former members of the R.C.M.P., and retired employees of the Canadian National Railways. I regret very much that all the minister has done since he became minister of this very important department is to tell me that he would refer the matter to the president of the Canadian National Railways, and that the president of the Canadian National Railways had given a certain reply. I know the matter was taken up in the presence of Mr. Donald Gordon in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, when Mr. Gordon appeared before that committee this year, but so far the government has washed its hands of this whole matter. I say to my hon. friend that there are some retired Canadian National employees in Winnipeg who still remember when the Minister of Transport was a Winnipeger, and they are surprised that he seems

to be doing no better with respect to this subject than some of his predecessors have done.
Mr. Chairman, I said I would co-operate by not taking up much time, but I hope when the minister gets the floor to make a speech he will have something important to say about these two important subjects.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make only a few remarks about grade crossings. Although there would be much to say on that matter, my observations will be brief.
The government should undertake a large program in order to eliminate grade crossings which are still numerous in Canada and especially in the province of Quebec.
Besides, grade crossings cost many lives and are the cause of quite large material damages that Canadian citizens have to pay for because, generally, the railways are never responsible for those accidents.
For instance, the C.P.R. line crosses the community where I live and the highway at six different points, over a distance of three miles. In the dead centre of the town of Lac Megantic, there is a grade crossing at the crossroad of four main streets and of the highway. Every year, we have to regret the loss of human lives and heavy material damages at that crossing.
The authorities of Lac Megantic have been making pressures and representations on that matter for some 30 years. They have a very thick file on this and it seems quite difficult to obtain anything because, to date, nothing was done concerning that grade crossing.
That is why I am suggesting to the minister, and this is quite possible, to come to an agreement with the Minister of Public Works regarding those grade crossings.
The C.P.R., the federal and provincial governments, and the municipalities should take advantage of the winter works program to remove those various grade crossings.
It seems to me that many municipalities do not know how to spend money earmarked for winter works and waste considerable amounts in unnecessary winter works. It would be much better if the money was spent to eliminate such crossings; it would serve a good cause and improve the situation considerably.
I think something should be done in that regard.
Supply-Transport
In the town of Megantic, taxpayers lose a considerable amount of time whenever a train blocks traffic.
There are three such crossings right in the centre of Megantic. Shunting operations are carried out right in the middle of the street, which thus becomes practically impassable. Very seldom can one go over the tracks without having to wait five, 10 or 15 minutes.
I believe the town of Megantic intends to insist on the elimination of that level crossing.
I call on the minister to do all in his power to carry out, not only in Megantic but throughout Canada, a vast program to remove level crossings which take a heavy toll in human lives. Human life is priceless and the government must do something, because nothing can replace such a great and noble gift.
I should now like to say a few words about radio broadcasting in my city.
The federal government has a small radio transmitter in Megantic, but reception is almost nil. In the daytime, we pick up the C.B.C. fairly well, but from 7, 8, 9, and 10 p.m., it is almost impossible to get that station. Since American stations interfere with the C.B.C. network, local citizens would be very grateful to the Minister of Transport if he could do something about it.
The small radio transmitter in our city might not be powerful enough. At any rate, reception is quite unsatisfactory, and I do not know exactly why. I was asked to report the matter to the Minister of Public Works and to ask him whether it would not be possible to effect some improvements in our small radio station.
I repeat what I have already told the minister: An agreement should be reached with the other departments so that we can get rid of railway crossings under the winter works program. In my opinion, that would be a great improvement throughout the country and that would do a great service to municipalities in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada.
If such an agreement were possible, a large number of towns in my constituency could undertake the elimination of grade crossings under the winter works program. That would be a very useful means for people generally to spend the money set aside for those works.

I realize the minister wants to get the floor and answer some of the questions that have been asked, so I shall do my best to co-operate and make my remarks very brief. I shall deal with a subject with

Supply-Transport
which I have dealt a number of times during the 12 years I have been a member of this house. It is a subject that is becoming of increasing importance every year. I refer to the search and rescue organizations on the great lakes. I confine my remarks to the great lakes because they are international waters over which the federal government has appropriate jurisdiction. The regulations that have been drawn up by the Department of Transport under the Canada Shipping Act apply to other waters as well, so I shall direct my remarks to the great lakes themselves.
I have found that every minister of transport over the years, starting with Hon. Mr. Marler and succeeding ministers, has been very helpful with this matter. They have all done something. I should like particularly to pay a compliment to the deputy minister of transport, Mr. Baldwin, who has spent a great deal of time dealing with matters such as this. At the moment there are a number of groups, governmental and non-governmental, on the great lakes which provide search and rescue organizations. In the non-governmental category, I refer to power boat squadrons and certain private fishing boats that are agreeable to assisting in connection with this matter. There are of course provincial police organizations, chiefly in the province of Ontario, municipal police and the like. There are other groups that I should like to mention as well, but time does not permit.
One of the principal jobs during the summer months on the great lakes is trying to co-ordinate these search and recue facilities. This is of course strictly a seasonal job. As I mentioned earlier, it is becoming increasingly important because of the number of small boats on the great lakes. I should not like to give a figure because I do not know, but I would estimate that the number of these boats has increased 10 or 20 times since the end of world war II. I know of one place, for instance, on lake Erie, namely Long Point, where on the opening day of the fishing season there will be approximately 3,000 or 4,000 boats going out into very dangerous and rough water. There is an increasing number of drownings on the great lakes every year.
Since this work is of a seasonal nature, chiefly during June, July, August and perhaps early September, the department would not be justified in going to the expense of employing people for this job on a year round basis. This is clearly not necessary. Perhaps during the summer months students from universities could be employed on this job as coordinators between existing search and rescue

services, from the Royal Canadian Air Force down to the power boat squadrons I mentioned. I think a great deal of good would be done. When an accident occurs many people do not know with whom they should get in touch. Time is of the essence in these situations and sometimes five or ten minutes can make the difference between life and death.
Five or ten minutes could make the difference between the saving of lives, and deaths in drowning accidents, and if these co-ordinators could be placed at the principal resort and boating points on lake Huron, Georgian bay, lake Erie and lake Ontario they would be a great help. Most university students finish their courses in May and they could undertake a three week training.
This would only be a seasonal job, but that is all that is necessary in this particular situation. It is part of the government's program to assist more students to go to universities. Hon. members know the difficulties students have in obtaining summer jobs, and the more students go to universities the more jobs they will need. The government could kill two jobs with one stone. Perhaps that is an unfortunate metaphor but I think the minister gets the general idea, that the plan I outline could be of assistance to students who require summer work and at the same time it would add to the safety factor on the great lakes.
In addition to training, these students might also be given certain law enforcement authority because we all know that a number of people of all ages, and they are not confined to teenagers-sometimes they are old teenagers of 40 and 50 years-get hold of power boats and rip in among people swimming near the shore, thus creating a great hazard. While regulations do exist providing for action to be taken against these people, their enforcement has been difficult, and it would be helpful if the co-ordinators were given power to enforce the regulations and deal with people who are reckless and careless of human life and limb when other people are swimming.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question I would like to bring up again with the minister. It is about four and a half months since I raised it first and at that time he said he would take it into consideration, but since then I have heard nothing about it. It is a purely local problem. Why is the same rent charged by the D.O.T. for Yorkton footage as is charged at Regina, when you consider the facilities at both airports?

I have written to the minister's department three times and I have never had an acknowledgement of my letters. Most of the other departments at least acknowledge my letters-they may tell me to jump over the moon, but at least they acknowledge them.

Before the hon. member for Winnipeg North speaks perhaps I may be allowed to apologize to the hon. member for Yorkton. To the best of my knowledge his letters have not been brought to my attention and I have no intention of being discourteous. I am very sorry he has not had an answer.
I hope the minister will take this under immediate consideration as the problem still exists and the people of Yorkton are incensed.

The first matter I want to refer to is the T.C.A. repair base in Winnipeg. I do not intend to put the history of that base on the record again, nor the changes which have been made at that base. This matter has been discussed on a number of occasions and the minister must know that the citizens of Manitoba, regardless of what economic group they come from, regardless of the party they represent, are unanimous in their feeling that Winnipeg has been treated shabbily by the management of T.C.A.
I want to put on the record just one illustration of why Manitoba feels the way it does. In February 1949, when T.C.A. announced that it was moving its operations administration staff from Winnipeg to Montreal-some 155 people-the president of T.C.A., Mr. Gordon McGregor, issued a statement in which he said in part:
There is no conceivable reason, nor any grounds for suspicion, that this move marks the beginning of a mass transfer of T.C.A. activities from Winnipeg to Montreal.
But of course since that time there have been mass transfers of various T.C.A. departments from Winnipeg to Montreal. However, it is not my intention to go into them in detail.
Hon. members will recall that big delegations came to Ottawa to make representations about this matter, that they saw the Prime Minister, that the Prime Minister and the former minister of transport made statements, and that both statements were interpreted in Winnipeg by everyone, including that old friend of the minister, the Winnipeg Free Press, as a commitment that no more changes would be made until further studies were undertaken. Finally the government agreed to the appointment of a one man commission
Supply-Transport
to investigate the whole question of T.C.A. operations in Winnipeg.
At present the various organizations in Manitoba which made representations previously wish to make representations to this one man commission. It was understood that the Manitoba government would get a copy of the Dixon-Speas report-not the edited version but the original report with all the information contained in it-so that it could put its experts to work in order that it could make the fullest and fairest representations to the one man commission.
It was understood this commission would begin its hearings in October, but according to a report which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on September 4, Arthur Mauro, the Manitoba government's transportation counsel, said that as of that date the Manitoba government had not yet received a copy of the report. I shall read a sentence of an exact quote from Mr. Mauro:
We are concerned about the delay because we were promised a copy of the report when the commission was established more than two months ago. Mr. Thompson, the commissioner, is doing everything possible to get us a copy of the report so we don't expect the holdup to last much longer.
There may be a reasonable explanation for this, but I want to warn the minister that the people of Manitoba have had so many explanations from T.C.A. that they have lost practically all their faith in the president of T.C.A., and I would urge the minister to make inquiries, if he has not already done so, to see that that report is turned over to the Manitoba government as quickly as possible.
The other matter I would like to raise is one which I expected the minister to deal with when he introduced the resolution preceding the bill to implement some of the recommendations of the MacPherson commission report. I refer to the fact that last year the house had before it a bill introduced by my hon. friend from Port Arthur, Bill No. C-15 to amend the Railway Act. The purpose of that measure was to provide that railway employees who lost their employment as a result of changes beneficial to a railway should be compensated by that railway for the cost of rehabilitating themselves with new skills saleable on the labour market. This bill must have had a lot of appeal because instead of being talked out, as are 99 per cent of the bills brought in by private members, it was sent to a special committee-*

To be talked out there.

Supply-Transport

The hon. member for Timmins says "to be talked out there". The fact is that the committee held a large number of meetings, heard evidence from the railway companies, from the railway unions and from other interested parties and then made a report which was virtually unanimous recommending in essence that sympathetic consideration should be given to the bill. I do not wish to enter now into the arguments which were presented. Hon. members are aware of the background of this measure. I might point out that the number of railway workers covered by non-operating labour unions in 1962 was 152,000. This year the unions are negotiating for 102,000 workers, the figure having been reduced by almost one third. This is what has happened, and nobody questions the right of the companies to reduce staff in accordance with changing methods so that the operation may be as efficient as possible. Nobody questions the need to do this. But we have now reached a position where, because of new methods of operation, the dieselization program, the use of steel freight cars, automatic hump yards, computing equipment which has eliminated a great deal of paper work, and, I would add, because of the kind of legislation we are to be asked to consider in detail to implement the recommendations of the MacPherson commission, these reductions in staff will probably continue for a considerable time.
I do not wish at this time to discuss the provisions of this bill brought in by my hon. friend from Port Arthur, because we shall have an opportunity of doing so on another occasion. But it does seem strange to me that neither today when we are discussing the estimates of his department nor the other day when he introduced a resolution preceding another railway measure, did the minister take the opportunity to indicate the government's view on the important principle contained in the measure which the hon. member for Port Arthur put forward last year, namely that railway workers, particularly those who have put in long years of service, should not be displaced from employment in consequence of technological changes or because of branch line abandonment programs at an age when it is virtually impossible for them to find other jobs. I maintain that the companies have an obligation both moral and legal to look after people who have worked for them and who have given their best years to the service of the railways. I should like the minister to give us some indication of the

government's view on this question. I do not expect the hon. gentleman to say: This is a very good bill which the hon. member for Port Arthur has introduced and we intend to bring it along. I do not expect any government to process a bill proposed by a member of another party. But it seems to me the minister should at least indicate the general policy the government has in mind with respect to this question, a question which affects the well-being and the livelihood of tens of thousands of workers in this country.

I see I have only the time left which is allotted to a private member. If therefore my remarks in reference to some of the points which have been raised are brief, I hope hon. members will not mind. In order to avoid turning the pages of my notes back and starting again, perhaps the hon. member for Three Rivers will forgive me if I leave his observations to the last; he will remember what was said in the gospel about that-and I do not mean to apply the same precept to the hon. member who has just spoken.
I should like to deal with the points he raised. I read the same piece in the Winnipeg Free Press as he did and I am making inquiries to find out why the Manitoba government has not yet received the Dixon-Speas report. As soon as I have the information I will let the hon. gentleman know why it was.
Let the Manitoba government know, not me.

The Manitoba government will probably find out as soon as I do. I am sure they are grateful to the hon. gentleman for acting as their porte parole in this house. As for the introduction last year of the bill by the hon. member for Port Arthur, I am not sure whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North was a member of the railway committee or not, but I indicated very clearly, I thought, the position which I took, and which the government took, on this matter. The questions involved in the hon. member's bill are of such far-reaching importance, affecting automation not merely in the railways but in the whole of the economy, that we felt they required a good deal more study than the committee had been able to give to the matter during the last session of parliament. The Department of Labour is studying this whole question and I am hopeful that as a result of these studies some constructive suggestions will be made to deal with this problem, which is primarily the responsibility of the

Department of Labour rather than of the Department of Transport. I may say in passing that in the bill which I was privileged to introduce the other day I recommended that parliament should restore what most people believed to be the law until the supreme court decided otherwise. This action would go some distance in the direction the hon. gentleman recommends. But we do not feel at the present time, having in mind the implications in relation to other occupations, that without additional study we could recommend going further at this particular time. But I would not like anyone to think we do not realize that this problem is, in many ways, the biggest which faces an industrial society.
The hon. member for Yorkton asked a question about an attempt to charge a relatively small place such as Yorkton the same amount as was charged in Regina. That is something I feel very regretful about neglecting and I will try to get an answer as soon as possible.
I was much interested by the suggestion of the hon. member for Oxford, and the fact that he related it to my ancestral home was perhaps not entirely accidental. I will certainly see that his suggestion is considered.
The hon. member for Compton-Frontenac and several other hon. members talked about the desirability of eliminating grade crossings. I think anyone who reads the newspapers or listens to the radio at any week end will realize how important is this subject. I do hope we can continue to make as much progress as possible in this connection. As for the problem of radio reception to which the hon. member referred, I will see that it is looked into.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised two subjects, one of which I do not intend to deal with until I come to the hon. member for Three Rivers, who raised it first. It will be the last topic with which I shall deal, and I hope to leave most of my time to deal with it. On the question of the retired C.N.R. employees, the hon. member described me as a messenger boy. Well, Mr. Chairman, I have nothing against messenger boys; I have carried many messages in my time. But the hon. gentleman does raise a question on which I suspect he and I would never be able to see eye to eye, no matter how long we lived; because I have never been able to convince myself that because someone had spent most of his working life on the public payroll and had then retired, he was entitled to consideration above that given by the general policies of the government to other
Supply-Transport
citizens who had retired, but in some cases were not even fortunate enough to have as
good a situation as those people who, though their pensions admittedly are very inadequate, were on the public payroll. It has always seemed to me that our social security policies should apply in similar circumstances to all sections of the population.
This may be because I have never represented a constituency in which there was a considerable number of these employees, and I do represent a constituency where the incomes are not very high and where there are very few people who receive pensions at all except the old age pension, which everyone gets uniformly. However, Mr. Chairman, I have always felt it was better to try to raise the level of social security for older people equally, for all kinds of older people, regardless of who their previous employer might be, and that it was rather difficult to find an equitable justification for singling out certain people because at one time they happened to be employed directly or indirectly by the state. I know the hon. member does not agree with that view. I do not think either of us would convince the other. He is perhaps right in saying that I have not been very zealous about the matter; but I am at least being honest about it.
The hon. member for Rosthern wants to stretch out navigation at Churchill. I would tell the hon. member that long before he was born I belonged to the "On to the Bay" association, and if there is one thing that stirs my imagination from my boyhood days it is navigation through Hudson bay. Whatever else I may be as Minister of Transport I am bound always to be an enthusiast for that particular route; even after visiting the place, as I did during the Easter holidays. My visit was short, I might add.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You must have been in short pants, too.

During the Easter holidays? No, it was in short breath. I am not sure that the best way of extending the season at Churchill is not perhaps to handle a greater volume in the season when the ships now operate, rather than trying to extend the number of months in the season. It might add up to the same thing. But there are very difficult technical problems. That does not mean we are not going to try to keep on solving them, because we solve new technical problems all the time.

Supply-Transport
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox talked about the citizens' radio band and the seals that are put on the radios of United States tourists. I am happy to say this matter was brought to my attention some weeks ago, and this policy has been changed, notwithstanding the fact that the United States will not reciprocate and still puts seals on our radios. As for the hon. gentleman's references to the competition between the railways and trucking, I think we are going to have many other opportunities of discussing this subject.
That brings me to the hon. member for Medicine Hat and his interesting suggestions about how to deal with the railway bill. I am going to make one suggestion myself. Since everyone else has been transgressing the rules, perhaps you will let me do the same, Mn Chairman, unless someone objects very strongly. I am going to suggest that it probably will not be feasible, having regard to the other matters that are coming before this house, to have the railway bill come back for second reading in the month of September. It might therefore be very desirable if we could have a totally informal series of meetings which would not be meetings of the oommittee as such, but of members of the railway committee or such hon. members as may wish to attend. Any hon. member who is not a member of the committee could attend these meetings if he wished to do so. Perhaps these meetings could be held in private, so that a lot of positions would not be taken up. In this event, Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to make available certain of the officials of my department to be asked questions about the bill. I think if that were done in an entirely informal way-perhaps you might call it a sort of seminar or study group: I know I sometimes made fun of these things when on the other side of the house, but they have their purpose-something useful might be achieved in this respect. This is a highly complex piece of legislation, and no one is more anxious to get it dealt with expeditiously and at the same time properly by the house than I am. If a number of hon. members who are members of the railway committee would like to indicate to me, to my parliamentary secretary or-though I have not had a chance to speak to him yet -the hon. member for Ottawa East that they would be interested in this kind of project, I would be very glad to see if we could organize it.

I think it would be much better to have a debate about what the bill really means than to have misapprehensions in the minds of hon. members in trying to decipher its legal language. I confess quite frankly that when I read the bill the first time, before I had a little instruction, I was rather confused by a great part of it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You had a head start.

Well, necessarily. I will be very happy if anyone can catch up; and I will not be very surprised. I am going to beg off any attempt to make a speech tonight about highway transport, having been warned by the hon. member for Rosthem that I am trying to do far too much and am spreading myself far too thinly over too many things. I think I should leave alone a subject that is not part of my responsibilities at all.
I will come to the subject of regional air services again at the close of my remarks. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, after paying a tribute to the amazing growth of that city which is apparently growing faster than any other in Canada, or at least in the province of Quebec, asked for a few tunnels, and one in particular. I will tell the C.N.R. about this and I will endeavour to earn his gratitude. I hope he will be as forthcoming about the flag as I am about his tunnel.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Order.
Bribery and corruption.

The hon. member for Sim-coe East asked one or two questions about pilots. I do not pretend to carry this information in my head; a messenger boy has brought me this little note. I am advised that we do have rules for medical examinations applicable to all pilots, and they vary depending on the category of the pilot. Permissible flying hours also vary according to the individual company but they are reviewed from time to time by the air transport board as a part of the company's operating certificate, and pilots must be examined medically once a year. If the hon. member wishes more details we will be very glad to let him have them.
The hon. member asked about grain elevators and whether the same service is provided to elevators owned by private companies as elevators owned by the C.N.R. I am not sure whether the C.N.R. does own any elevators, but I think the hon. gentleman means elevators owned one way or another by some public agency. I should have thought

that so far as any general services of the Department of Transport are concerned they would be quite the same, but the main services he would probably be interested in would be dredging and that sort of thing, which is not my responsibility, of course, but the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works. That would apply also to dredging generally. I will have to put a little pressure on the Minister of Public Works to do a little dredging this year in the great lakes because of the water levels.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre had some things to say about the grade crossing fund in so far as it affected Moose Jaw, and I will see that the board of transport commissioners have their attention directed to his observations. I will also have details given to him about this problem to which he referred, and they will be sent to him in writing.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert made one or two suggestions about how to deal with railway legislation along the lines which were elaborated a little more by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. He said that the national harbours board was a good thing and I think that was gratifying to me as well as to the board. The hon. member mentioned the harbour bridge in Saint John. I do not think anything will contribute more to the economy of Saint John than the building of the harbour bridge, and I can tell him that I personally am very sympathetic toward doing everything I can so that that project is proceeded with as quickly as possible.
Whether or not having a Department of Transport weather forecaster at the Saint John airport would make people happier when planes did not come in I am not absolutely sure, but at any rate we will give the matter careful consideration. I know the hon. member's interest in the merchant navy. I share it, but perhaps not quite with the same degree of enthusiasm as he, as I am sure he is the most enthusiastic member in the house, at least on that side of the house, on this matter. I also know his views about winter navigation. There is a problem there of balancing one part of the country with another and balancing the interests of both, which is not easy to do.
As for the constructive suggestions made by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra concerning Vancouver harbour, and particularly the grain handling facilities there, I may say I am very anxious to see the expansion of the grain handling facilities and the
Supply-Transport
facilities for handling bulk cargo generally in Vancouver harbour. Anything I can reasonably do to push that ahead will be done.
I feel very sad about those lobsters to which the hon. member for York-Scarborough referred; I hope they were not dead before the party. We are looking into his problem about the delivery of express, and we are trying to solve all of the problems of Scarborough, including redistribution. The hon. member also referred to the monopoly of taxi and other services at the airports, as did several other hon. members. I think I dealt with this subject at some length in reply to an intervention by the hon. member for Burnaby-Co-quitlam when we were considering interim supply some time ago, and I do not think I can usefully add anything to what I said on that occasion. I forget the page in Hansard in this regard, but I am sure hon. members can look it up. It is an awkward problem, and I certainly agree with what everyone has said about it-that as long as people have any kind of monopoly they have to be watched.
The hon. member for Quebec East said he thought the job of Minister of Transport was too big for any one man. I am not sure that I entirely disagree with that, but notwithstanding the excellent schemes which have been put forward for dividing up the department, if you are going to try, as we are trying in the legislation we are now putting forward, to look at the transportation problems with which parliament has to deal as a whole and try to get some co-ordination, it is frightfully difficult to separate the department. Perhaps when we get some of these policies better worked out it might be possible. Personally I should like to carve off some of the peripheral parts of the department and get rid of them if I could; but it is really a problem for the Prime Minister, not for me, as I have enough of my own, as I have been told.
The situation in the railways in Quebec city to which the hon. member for Quebec East referred is being pursued assiduously by my hon. friend the hon. member for Quebec South, my parliamentary secretary. He is very zealous about these matters and I am sure they can safely be left in his hands. I think that applies to most of the questions, except the one about the television in Gaspe which was raised by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency. However, I think I should say that my hon. friend for Quebec South and I have more faith in the growth of the harbour at Quebec than the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency showed. We

Supply-Transport
believe there is going to be a very great expansion of that harbour in the next 20 years and we want to be very careful not to inhibit our capacity to expand. At the same time the problem of the Beaupre shore to which the hon. member referred is being considered very actively indeed at the present time. I will try to get together as quickly as I can such statistics as are available to us which the hon. gentleman wanted, and furnish him with them.
With regard to the problem about the television, I really think this is outside the scope of my responsibilities in any event. This being the case I am not going to say anything more about it tonight.
I come now to the observations of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who had some complimentary things to say about the air transport board and its operations. I have no doubt that it was partly as a result of his urging that they did have a hearing in British Columbia, and I am sure that it is a very good thing for these governmental agencies to see on the spot what are the conditions which prevail whenever it is possible to do so. I must say that the question of the flaw in the Aeronautics Act, or what the hon. gentleman thought was a flaw, is something I will have looked at, and perhaps if we ever get to that bill something might be done about it. With regard to the matter of facilities for water landings for planes, the hon. gentleman is not wrong in thinking that this matter is a matter of real interest to me. I have landed in planes in some of the most unlikely places along a coast that is almost as difficult as the hon. gentleman's coast. This is one of the matters which we have to tackle more earnestly than we have up to the present.
The submission of the British Columbia aviation council, which was given to me when I was performing another function as commodore of the Kelowna regatta, is being studied at the present time by the department.
In respect of many of the things about these wharf charges, to which the hon. member referred, I at any rate have a feeling of sympathy, if I do not agree in total with them. It was perhaps not the most auspicious part of my beginning as Minister of Transport, that just before I began there was a complete overhaul of these wharfage charges. This did create the impression in my own constituency that my first act as Minister of Transport was to charge more for the use of wharves, which, perhaps if I had control of the timing,

might have been done a little differently. However, I think the hon. gentleman can be pretty sure that on this subject I will tend to be on the side of the users of the wharves, just as far as one can and still have some regard for the public interest. At any rate, the regulations with regard to wharves are not, in my view, as the laws of the Medes and Persians, but are subject to change almost without notice if I can think of any good reason for changing them.
I do not think I will attempt to add anything to what I said about community antenna television on July 22, which the hon. member can reread at page 5799 of Hansard. I have no new views on the subject since I gave those on that date. In view of what the hon. gentleman said about television reception in certain parts of his constituency he ought to get together with the hon. member for Kootenay East. I suggest that they make a joint attack on the C.B.C. in respect of this matter and, at any rate, they will carry my sympathy with them.
I come at last to the remarks of the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I intend to take in opposite order the items to which he referred, dealing first with the problem in respect of the use of our waters and the conservation of our waters. I do not think I should really attempt at this stage to add anything to what I said in reply to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce on orders of the day. I should very much like to see the agreement of the house leaders, who seem to be very agreeable these days, to put through the motion to have this reference to the committee, so that we can have a good look at what is now being done in the country and at what some of these problems are during this session. I think that would help a great deal to understand this better and to enlist greater support from the house generally for what needs to be done.
The hon. member referred to a reserving of the business of northern supply for ships on Canadian registry. I think the hon. gentleman is perhaps not unaware of the fact that I got my fingers slightly burned in this particular traffic and I will probably be a little more careful next time.
About cabotage, the Senate has given its blessings to the policy suggested by the hon. gentleman, when he was minister, in a bill that is now on the order paper, and that, God willing, we will reach some time before Christmas.
I hope in the near future to be able to make a rather detailed statement about ship-

building and this whole matter. There has been a great deal of shipbuilding done because of the subsidy policy introduced by the hon. member for Three Rivers. I think the time has come to make a thorough appraisal of the results of that policy. Certainly one of the results has been a vast increase in employment in shipyards, for which we are all very grateful.
I do not think I will say anything more about bus and taxi services at airports.
I now come to the general question of air policy. I think I ought to start by recalling to the hon. gentleman that I have not got much more than three minutes left at this time. The last time I attempted to do this these three minutes were taken up by others and I had to accept an invitation from the C.B.C., and that is the only time I have ever been on, so the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam does not need to feel that he is the only one who is left out. Perhaps this evening the committee will be more inclined to listen to me even, though this is only repetition.
The principles recommended as a basis for civil aviation policy are:
(1)	In the international field, air services provided by Canadian air lines should serve the Canadian interest as a whole; these services should not be competitive or conflicting, but should represent a single integrated plan, which could be achieved by amalgamation, by partnership or by a clear division of fields of operations.
(2)	In the domestic main line field, while the principle of competition is not rejected, any development of competition should not compromise or seriously injure the economic viability of T.C.A.'s main line domestic operations which represent the essential framework of its network of domestic services. In other words, there must not be the kind of competition which would put T.C.A. into the red; and, in the event that competition continues, the air transport board should ensure an opportunity for growth to both lines above this basic minimum.
(3)	In formulation of policy based upon the foregoing point, a reasonable role for regional air carriers providing scheduled and regular air service must be established; this role must provide for a relationship between the regional air carriers and T.C.A. (and any other licensed main line transcontinental carrier) which will give the regional air carriers a reasonable chance to operate without government subsidies.
Supply-Transport
If I could have three minutes more and the committee saw fit to listen to me I think I could conclude these observations.
Agreed.

I asked the two air lines to hold discussions to see within this framework whether they could come up with some agreed recommendations. I hope that they will have, at any rate, reached agreement on a great many points by the end of September. On some points they have already reached full agreement. I believe that a lot of the conflicting difficulty outside Canada has already been solved. However, I do feel that the greater the measure of consent and agreement we can get in these matters, rather than the imposition of policy from above, the more likely it is to work smoothly and effectively.
I am also very much impressed with the fact that it took, to my personal knowledge, a year and a half at least, and maybe longer,, before the policy that was formulated in those general lines by Mr. Mackenzie King, and extended in 1944 by Mr. C. D. Howe, was-worked out. My own view is that that policy, even with some erosion of which I did not approve, I might add, has served this country pretty well for 20 years. I am more anxious to see that any policies I recommend to my colleagues, and that my colleagues join in recommending to this house, will work for 20 years, than in trying to meet some deadline of September 30 or October 31. What we want to do is to get a policy that is right for this country. If it takes two or three extra months to do it, so far as I am concerned I think I would be wiser to take the two or three extra months. I do believe that this framework which was announced on May 1, and with which I found very little quarrel in any part of the country, is on the whole the right framework within which to work out this policy.
I do agree, too, that there has to be a proper balance between the one or two main line carriers, whichever there are going to be -I am talking about the domestic field at the moment-and the regional carriers. I do not believe that one great, single carrier can perform all the scheduled air service for this country satisfactorily. I think the headquarters would be too far from the field. For a regional scheduled carrier to operate effectively, his headquarters have got to be in the area of his operation. I say this not from any theoretical standpoint. Anybody who has been a politician in Newfoundland in the period I have been, when at the start you

Supply-Transport
did not have very many roads, who has seen now dependant a region can be on air services for the essential services, knows that a regional service could not be effectively provided from Montreal. I think that would be even truer of British Columbia, which is still farther away.
I think we have to get a proper balance. It is very important to get that balance in such a way that, so far as possible, the users and not the taxpayers pay for the service. This does not mean that there may not be air services so essential to the national interest that they have to be provided even if they will not pay. However we do have to get this balance. We are going to get it, but it is not going to be easy and it is not going to be achieved next week. I am going to keep right on pushing just as hard as I can for the achievement of this, which I think is every bit as important as the railway legislation. The government, as all hon. members know, has made firm recommendations to parliament in this railway legislation. These firm recommendations do not mean that every comma in that bill has got to stay as it is. There would be no sense in sending it to a committee, there would be no sense in studying it in advance or having subcommittees, if that were our attitude. We do believe, however, that along broad lines we have made good recommendations. I hope before the end of this year I will be able to make good recommendations, too, about air policy.
Now, I was just wondering, since we have had a broad ranging discussion, if the committee might feel inclined to carry the first
item of my estimates. Then, all specific questions could be dealt with on specific items.

Item agreed to.

speechtext: That is enough.

I am grateful to the committee. I am glad no one minded too much my not making a speech at the beginning.
Progress reported.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
